language.name: Express.js
language.description: The backend framework of the MERN stack. Covers routing, middleware, requests and responses, error handling, validation and file uploads, authentication, security, API design and project structure, testing and deployment.

questions.question: What does a minimal Express server look like, and what does each line do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Five lines are enough: import Express, create an app, add a route, and start listening on a port. Think of the app as a restaurant, routes as the menu, and listen() as opening the doors.

How it works:
require('express'): loads the library
express(): creates the app object that holds routes and middleware
app.get(path, handler): runs the handler when a GET request hits that path
res.json(): sends a JSON response and ends the request
app.listen(port): starts the HTTP server and waits for requests

Example: Run node server.js, open http://localhost:5000/api/health in the browser and you see { "status": "ok" }. That is your first working API, and real projects grow from exactly this file.

Common mistake: Forgetting to send a response. If the handler never calls res.json() or res.send(), the browser keeps loading until it times out.

Interview tip: Add that in real projects you keep app.js (routes and middleware) separate from server.js (listen), so tests can import the app without opening a port.

questions.question: What are the req and res objects in an Express route handler?
questions.answer:
Short answer: req (request) is everything the client sent: URL, headers, body, cookies. res (response) is your toolkit to answer back: status code, headers and data. Like an order slip you read and a tray you send back.

How it works: Most used parts:
req.params: values from the URL path, like :id
req.query: values after the ?, like ?page=2
req.body: data sent in POST or PUT (needs express.json())
req.headers: for example the Authorization header
res.status(): sets the HTTP status code
res.json(): sends JSON and finishes the response

Example: For POST /api/courses with body { "title": "Express 101" }, your handler reads req.body.title, saves the course and replies res.status(201).json(course).

Common mistake: Sending two responses in one handler, for example res.json() inside an if and another res.json() after it without return. The second one crashes with "Cannot set headers after they are sent".

Interview tip: Mention that req and res are Node's own request and response objects with extra helpers that Express adds on top.

questions.question: What is the difference between app.use(), app.get() and app.all()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: app.get() matches only GET requests on an exact path. app.all() matches every HTTP method on that path. app.use() mounts middleware for every method on a path prefix, so "/api" also matches "/api/users".

How it works:
app.get('/users'): GET /users only
app.all('/users'): GET, POST, PUT, DELETE and more on /users
app.use('/api', fn): any method, any path starting with /api
Inside app.use: req.path has the prefix removed, req.originalUrl keeps the full URL

Example: app.use('/api', apiLimiter) rate-limits the whole API. app.all('/old-endpoint', (req, res) => res.status(410).json({ message: 'Gone' })) answers every method on a removed endpoint.

Common mistake: Using app.use('/', handler) to send a response, thinking it is a homepage route. It matches every request, so all your later routes become unreachable.

Interview tip: Say app.use is for middleware and mounting routers, while app.get and friends are for endpoints. That one sentence shows you understand how the request pipeline is built.

questions.question: How do you serve a React (Vite) build from an Express server, including client-side routes like /dashboard?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Serve the dist folder with express.static(), then add a fallback that sends index.html for any non-API GET request, so React Router can handle the page.

How it works:
express.static('client/dist'): serves JS, CSS and images
API routes first: /api/... must be registered before the fallback
Fallback: any other GET returns index.html, React Router reads the URL

Example: A user refreshes on /dashboard. There is no file called dashboard, so without the fallback Express returns 404. With it, index.html loads and React shows the dashboard page.

Common mistake: Putting the fallback before the API routes. Then GET /api/courses returns HTML instead of JSON, and the frontend fails with "Unexpected token <".

Interview tip: Mention the trade-off: one server is simple and has no CORS issues, while hosting the frontend on Vercel and the API on Render (like many MERN apps) scales and deploys each part separately.

questions.question: What is the difference between "npm start" and "npm run dev" in an Express project, and how do nodemon or node --watch help?
questions.answer:
Short answer: npm start usually runs node server.js for production. npm run dev runs a watcher that restarts the server every time you save a file, so you do not stop and start it by hand.

How it works:
"start": "node server.js" used by hosts like Render and Railway
"dev": "nodemon server.js" or "node --watch server.js" for development
node --watch: built into Node 18.11+, no extra package needed
npm run <name>: runs any script from package.json

Example: You change a route message and press save. The terminal shows "restarting..." and the next request returns the new text immediately.

Common mistake: Setting the production start command to nodemon. It adds a dev tool to production, watches files that never change, and nodemon may not even be installed if it is a devDependency.

Interview tip: Mention that you keep tools like nodemon, jest and eslint in devDependencies, and that hosts run npm install with production settings, so the start script must use plain node.

questions.question: What are app.locals and res.locals, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: app.locals holds values for the whole app's lifetime, shared by every request. res.locals holds values for one request only, a safe place to pass data between middleware.

How it works:
app.locals: set once at startup, like the app name or a config object
res.locals: set in middleware, read later in the same request
Templates: both are automatically available in views (EJS, Pug)

Example: An auth middleware loads the user and stores it in res.locals.user. A later middleware checks res.locals.user.role, and the route handler uses it to build the response.

Common mistake: Storing per-user data in app.locals. It is shared, so user A's data can leak into user B's request when many people use the app at once.

Interview tip: Mention that many teams use req.user instead of res.locals for the logged-in user. Both work, the key point is that per-request data must never live in a shared global.

questions.question: Your Express app works locally, but after deploying to Render the logs say "No open ports detected". What is wrong, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The app is listening on a hard-coded port like 5000, but the platform tells your app which port to use through the PORT environment variable. Listen on process.env.PORT.

How it works:
Platform: Render, Railway and Heroku set PORT and route traffic to it
Your code: app.listen(process.env.PORT || 5000)
Host: listen on all interfaces (the default), not only 127.0.0.1
Crash check: if the app crashes on start (missing env var, bad Mongo URI), no port opens either

Real example: A student deploys their portfolio API. It runs fine locally, but Render keeps restarting it. The fix is one line: process.env.PORT. A second cause was a missing MONGO_URI in Render's environment settings, so the app crashed before listen().

Common mistake: Looking for a bug in the routes. When no port opens, check the start logs from the top: env vars, database connection and the listen call.

Interview tip: Say you add a startup log line like "Listening on port 10000" and a /api/health route, so deploy problems show up in seconds.
questions.codeSnippet:
const PORT = process.env.PORT || 5000;
app.listen(PORT, () => console.log(`Listening on port ${PORT}`));

questions.question: How does Express handle a request internally, from the moment it arrives to the moment a response is sent?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express keeps one ordered list (a stack) of middleware and routes. Each request walks down that list from top to bottom. Every layer either sends a response or calls next() to pass the request on.

How it works:
Arrival: Node's http server gives Express the raw request
Matching: each layer checks if its path and method match
Running: matching middleware runs, then calls next() or responds
Routers: a mounted router has its own small stack inside
Errors: next(err) or a thrown error skips normal middleware and jumps to error handlers
End: if nothing responds, Express's final handler sends 404

Example: GET /api/courses passes cors, json parser, logger and the /api router, reaches the courses route, and res.json() ends it. Later middleware never runs.

Common mistake: Thinking routes run in parallel or "the best match wins". The first matching layer in registration order wins.

Interview tip: Draw it as a pipeline in the interview. Interviewers love candidates who can explain why order matters instead of just saying that it does.

questions.question: When would you choose Express over Fastify or NestJS for a new Node.js backend?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Choose Express for simple to medium APIs, fast learning and the biggest ecosystem. Choose Fastify when raw speed and built-in schema validation matter. Choose NestJS when a large team needs strict structure and TypeScript everywhere.

How it works:
Express: minimal and flexible, most tutorials and middleware, you design the structure yourself
Fastify: faster JSON handling and routing, JSON schema validation and a plugin system built in
NestJS: Angular-style modules, dependency injection, decorators, runs on Express or Fastify underneath

Real example: A startup MVP or a client portal like an interview prep site is quick to build in Express. A bank with 40 backend developers might pick NestJS so every module looks the same.

Common mistake: Picking a framework for benchmark numbers alone. For most apps the database is the slow part, not the framework.

Interview tip: Remote companies like candidates who know Express deeply and can explain trade-offs. Say "Express gave me the fundamentals, so moving to Fastify or NestJS is mostly learning their structure."

questions.question: What changes when you switch an Express project from CommonJS (require) to ES modules (import)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: You add "type": "module" to package.json and use import/export. Some CommonJS features disappear, like __dirname and require(), so you replace them.

How it works:
Imports: import express from 'express' instead of require('express')
Exports: export default router instead of module.exports
File paths: local imports need the extension, './routes/users.js'
__dirname: rebuild it with fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)
JSON files: use fs to read them, or import with { type: 'json' }

Example: After switching, path.join(__dirname, 'public') throws "__dirname is not defined". Two lines with fileURLToPath and path.dirname fix it.

Common mistake: Mixing both styles in one project, like require() inside an ES module file. Node throws "require is not defined in ES module scope".

Interview tip: Say both work fine with Express 5. Pick one style per project and keep it consistent. Many existing company codebases still use CommonJS, so you should be comfortable reading both.

questions.question: Which command adds Express to a Node.js project?
options: npm install express
node install express
npm create express
npx express start
questions.correctAnswer: npm install express
questions.answer:
Why A: npm install express downloads the package and saves it in package.json dependencies.

Why not B: node runs JavaScript files, it does not install packages.

Why not C: npm create runs a starter template, it is not how you add Express to an existing project.

Why not D: npx runs a package's command line tool, and Express has no "start" command.

questions.question: What Content-Type does Express set when a route calls res.send({ ok: true })?
options: text/html
text/plain
application/json
No Content-Type header at all
questions.correctAnswer: application/json
questions.answer:
Why C: When res.send() gets an object or array, Express turns it into JSON and sets application/json, just like res.json().

Why not A: text/html is used when you send a string.

Why not B: Express does not use text/plain for objects.

Why not D: Express always sets a Content-Type when it sends a body with res.send().

questions.question: Which line serves the files inside a "public" folder, like /logo.png?
options: app.get("/public", express.files())
app.use(express.static("public"))
app.static("public")
app.use("/public", res.sendFile)
questions.correctAnswer: app.use(express.static("public"))
questions.answer:
Why B: express.static() is built-in middleware that serves files from a folder, so public/logo.png is available at /logo.png.

Why not A: There is no express.files() function.

Why not C: app has no static() method. static belongs to express.

Why not D: res.sendFile is a response method used inside a handler, not a middleware you can mount.

questions.question: With default settings, does a route defined as app.get("/about") also answer a request to /about/ (with a trailing slash)?
options: No, it returns 404
No, Express redirects to /about first
Only in production mode
Yes, trailing slashes are ignored by default
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, trailing slashes are ignored by default
questions.answer:
Why D: Routing is not strict by default, so /about and /about/ are treated the same.

Why not A: A 404 happens only if you turn on strict routing.

Why not B: Express does not redirect, it simply matches the route.

Why not C: NODE_ENV does not change route matching.

questions.question: An app runs app.listen(5000) on a host that sets PORT=10000. What happens after deploy?
options: The host forwards port 10000 to 5000 automatically
The app works, because 5000 is the Express default
The host cannot reach the app, health checks fail and the deploy is marked unhealthy
Express reads PORT automatically and uses 10000
questions.correctAnswer: The host cannot reach the app, health checks fail and the deploy is marked unhealthy
questions.answer:
Why C: The host sends traffic to the port in PORT, but nothing listens there, so health checks fail.

Why not A: Hosts do not guess your port. They expect you to use the one they give.

Why not B: Express has no default port. You always choose it in listen().

Why not D: Express never reads environment variables by itself.

Fix: app.listen(process.env.PORT || 5000)

questions.question: A project has "type": "module" in package.json. What happens on the line path.join(__dirname, "public")?
options: It works the same as in CommonJS
It throws ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined
It returns the current working directory
It returns undefined/public
questions.correctAnswer: It throws ReferenceError: __dirname is not defined
questions.answer:
Why B: __dirname only exists in CommonJS modules. In ES modules it is not defined, so using it throws.

Why not A: ES modules do not create the __dirname variable.

Why not C: That is process.cwd(), a different thing that is still available.

Why not D: A missing variable throws an error, it does not become undefined.

Fix: const __dirname = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));

questions.question: How do you define routes for different HTTP methods in Express, and what does app.route() do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each HTTP method has its own function: app.get, app.post, app.put, app.patch and app.delete. app.route(path) lets you chain all methods for one path so you write the path only once.

How it works:
GET: read data
POST: create something new
PUT / PATCH: replace or partly update
DELETE: remove
app.route('/courses'): chain .get().post() on the same path

Example: A course API needs list and create on /api/courses, and read, update and delete on /api/courses/:id. With app.route() that is two short blocks instead of five separate lines that repeat the path.

Common mistake: Doing everything with GET, like GET /deleteCourse?id=5. Browsers, crawlers and link previews can call GET URLs on their own, so one shared link could delete data.

Interview tip: Mention that the method plus the path together identify an endpoint, so GET /courses and POST /courses are two different routes that can live side by side.
questions.codeSnippet:
router.route('/courses')
  .get(listCourses)
  .post(protect, createCourse);

router.route('/courses/:id')
  .get(getCourse)
  .patch(protect, updateCourse)
  .delete(protect, deleteCourse);

questions.question: How do you read a value from a URL like /courses/:slug, and what type is that value?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Name the dynamic part with a colon in the route path, then read it from req.params. The value is always a string, even when it looks like a number.

How it works:
Route: app.get('/courses/:slug', ...)
Request: GET /courses/express-basics
Value: req.params.slug is "express-basics"
Several params: '/users/:userId/posts/:postId' gives two keys

Example: GET /api/quiz/42 with route /api/quiz/:id gives req.params.id === "42". To do math or compare with a number you convert it first: Number(req.params.id).

Common mistake: Writing if (req.params.id === 42). The string "42" is never strictly equal to the number 42, so the check always fails.

Interview tip: Mention that you validate params before using them, for example checking that an id is a valid MongoDB ObjectId, and return 400 instead of letting the database throw a 500.

questions.question: How do you split a growing app.js into separate route files like /api/users and /api/courses?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create one express.Router() per feature in its own file, export it, and mount it in app.js with a path prefix. Each file then only knows its own small paths.

How it works:
routes/userRoutes.js: router.get('/me', ...) and other user routes
app.js: app.use('/api/users', userRoutes)
Result: GET /api/users/me reaches the router's '/me' route
Shared middleware: router.use(protect) protects every route in that file

Example: An app with auth, courses, quizzes and admin routes keeps app.js under 50 lines. A new teammate looking for the quiz endpoints opens routes/quizRoutes.js and finds them all there.

Common mistake: Repeating the prefix inside the router, like router.get('/api/users/me') while also mounting at '/api/users'. The real URL becomes /api/users/api/users/me.

Interview tip: Say routes should stay thin: path, middleware and a controller function. The logic lives in controllers and services, which keeps routes easy to read like a table of contents.

questions.question: A route GET /users/me always returns "User not found" even though the user is logged in. The router also has GET /users/:id. What is going on?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Route order. /users/:id is registered first and matches /users/me too, with id = "me". Express runs the first matching route, so /users/me is never reached.

How it works: Express checks routes from top to bottom. ":id" matches any single path segment, including words like "me", "stats" or "search". Then findById("me") fails, because "me" is not an ObjectId.

Example: Moving router.get('/me') above router.get('/:id') fixes it at once. The same rule applies to /courses/popular, /orders/export and similar fixed paths.

Common mistake: Fixing it inside the :id handler with if (req.params.id === 'me'). It works, but it hides the real problem and grows into a messy handler.

Interview tip: Say your rule: specific routes first, parameter routes after. You can also restrict a parameter's format with validation middleware so ":id" only accepts valid ObjectIds and passes other values on.
questions.codeSnippet:
router.get('/me', protect, getMe);   // specific first
router.get('/:id', getUserById);     // generic after

questions.question: How do you chain several middleware functions on a single route, and why is that useful?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Pass them in order before the final handler: router.post('/', protect, allowRoles('admin'), validate(schema), createCourse). Each one must call next() for the request to continue.

How it works:
Order: runs left to right, like checkpoints
Early exit: any step can send a 4xx response and stop the chain
Arrays: you can group them, const adminOnly = [protect, allowRoles('admin')]
Reuse: the same small functions protect many routes

Example: Creating a course needs a logged-in user, an admin role and a valid body. Each check is a tiny reusable function, and the controller only contains the "create" logic.

Common mistake: Writing all checks inside the controller. The controller becomes long and every new route copies the same 20 lines of auth and validation code.

Interview tip: Mention it follows the single responsibility idea: each middleware does one job, so it is easy to test and reuse. Remote reviewers notice this in take-home assignments.

questions.question: What does router.param() do, and how can you use it to validate route parameters?
questions.answer:
Short answer: router.param('id', fn) runs a function every time a route in that router has an :id parameter, before the route handler. It is a neat place to validate or preload data once instead of in every route.

How it works:
Runs once per request, even if several routes match
Receives (req, res, next, value)
Can call next() to continue, or send 400 or 404 to stop
Can attach data, like req.course, for the handlers

Example: In courseRoutes, router.param('id') checks the ObjectId and loads the course. GET, PATCH and DELETE handlers then just use req.course, and a wrong id returns 404 in one shared place.

Common mistake: Expecting router.param on the app to work for routes inside a mounted router. Param callbacks only apply to routes of the router (or app) where they are defined.

Interview tip: Mention the alternative many teams prefer: a small validateObjectId middleware added to the routes that need it, which is more explicit when reading the route list.

questions.question: How did wildcard and optional route paths change in Express 5, and how do you update old routes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express 5 uses a newer path-to-regexp. A bare * is no longer allowed: wildcards must be named, like /*splat, and optional parts use braces, like /:file{.:ext}. Regex characters such as ? and + in string paths are gone.

How it works:
Express 4 wildcard: app.get('*')
Express 5 wildcard: app.get('/*splat'), and req.params.splat is an array of segments
Include the root path too: '/{*splat}'
Optional parameter: '/users{/:id}' instead of '/users/:id?'
Real regex: still possible by passing a RegExp object

Example: Upgrading a MERN app, the server crashes on start with "Missing parameter name" at the SPA fallback app.get('*'). Changing it to app.get('/{*splat}') fixes it.

Common mistake: Upgrading Express with npm install and not starting the server to test. Old path strings fail at startup, so the error is easy to catch if you look.

Interview tip: Mention the other Express 5 changes in the same breath: async errors go to the error handler automatically, and req.query is now a read-only getter.

questions.question: How does Express parse query strings like ?tag=js&tag=node, and why can that be a security problem?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A repeated key becomes an array, so req.query.tag is ["js", "node"]. That means a value you expect to be a string can arrive as an array, which breaks code or creates injection risks if you trust it.

How it works:
Single key: ?page=2 gives "2", always a string
Repeated key: ?tag=a&tag=b gives an array
Express 5 default: the "simple" parser, no nested objects
Express 4 default: the "extended" parser (qs), where ?price[$gt]=0 becomes an object

Example: Code does req.query.email.toLowerCase(). An attacker sends ?email=a&email=b, the value is an array, toLowerCase is not a function, and the route crashes with a 500.

Common mistake: Passing req.query straight into a MongoDB filter, like User.find(req.query). With the extended parser, ?role[$ne]=user can turn into an operator and list admins.

Interview tip: Say you validate and cast every query value (express-validator, zod) and build filters only from whitelisted keys.

questions.question: In nested routes like /courses/:courseId/lessons, why is req.params.courseId undefined inside the lessons router, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A router only sees its own parameters by default. The :courseId belongs to the parent path, so the child router cannot read it. Create the child router with { mergeParams: true }.

How it works:
Parent: app.use('/api/courses/:courseId/lessons', lessonRouter)
Child: express.Router({ mergeParams: true })
Result: req.params has courseId plus the child's own params, like lessonId

Example: GET /api/courses/abc123/lessons should list lessons of course abc123. Without mergeParams, Lesson.find({ course: undefined }) returns nothing, and the bug looks like an empty course.

Common mistake: Working around it by parsing req.originalUrl by hand. It breaks as soon as the URL structure changes.

Interview tip: Mention that nesting deeper than two levels (/courses/:id/lessons/:id/comments/:id) usually becomes hard to use, and that flatter URLs like /comments?lessonId=... are often cleaner.

questions.question: How do you return a clean JSON 404 for unknown routes and a 405 when the path exists but the method is wrong?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Add a catch-all 404 middleware after all routes. For 405, add a route.all() at the end of each path's chain that responds with 405 and an Allow header listing the supported methods.

How it works:
404: app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json(...)) placed after every route
405: router.route('/courses').get(...).post(...).all(methodNotAllowed)
Allow header: tells clients which methods are valid, like "GET, POST"
Default Express: unknown routes return an HTML "Cannot GET /x" page

Example: A frontend developer calls PUT /api/courses by mistake. Instead of a confusing 404, they get 405 with Allow: GET, POST and fix it in a minute.

Common mistake: Registering the 404 middleware before the routers. Every request then returns 404.

Interview tip: Say a JSON 404 matters because API clients expect JSON. An HTML error page breaks res.json() parsing on the frontend with "Unexpected token <".

questions.question: Which call handles a PATCH request to /users/:id?
options: router.update("/users/:id", handler)
router.put.patch("/users/:id", handler)
router.method("PATCH", "/users/:id", handler)
router.patch("/users/:id", handler)
questions.correctAnswer: router.patch("/users/:id", handler)
questions.answer:
Why D: Express has one function per HTTP method, and patch() handles PATCH.

Why not A: There is no update() method on a router.

Why not B: put is a function, it has no patch property for routing.

Why not C: There is no generic method() function in Express routing.

questions.question: A router mounted at "/api" has the route "/users/:id". For GET /api/users/42, what is req.params.id?
options: The number 42
The string "42"
undefined, because of the /api prefix
The string "/42"
questions.correctAnswer: The string "42"
questions.answer:
Why B: Route parameters are always strings. The mount prefix does not change that.

Why not A: Express never converts params to numbers.

Why not C: The prefix is removed before matching, so the :id parameter is found normally.

Why not D: The slash is part of the path pattern, not the value.

questions.question: A router defines GET "/users/:id" and then GET "/users/me". What happens with a request to /users/me?
options: The "/users/:id" handler runs with id "me"
The "/users/me" handler runs because it is more specific
Both handlers run, one after the other
Express throws an error about conflicting routes
questions.correctAnswer: The "/users/:id" handler runs with id "me"
questions.answer:
Why A: Express checks routes in the order they were added. "/users/:id" matches first, with id set to "me".

Why not B: Express does not rank routes by how specific they are.

Why not C: Only the first handler runs, unless it calls next() on purpose.

Why not D: Overlapping routes are allowed. Express just uses the first match.

Fix: Register "/users/me" before "/users/:id".

questions.question: For the request GET /search?tag=js&tag=node, what is req.query.tag?
options: "node", the last value wins
"js", the first value wins
"js,node"
["js", "node"]
questions.correctAnswer: ["js", "node"]
questions.answer:
Why D: When a key repeats, Express's query parser collects all the values into an array.

Why not A: No value is dropped, so the last one does not "win".

Why not B: The first value is not kept alone either.

Why not C: Values are not joined into one string.

questions.question: After upgrading to Express 5, what happens with app.get("*", handler)?
options: It works the same as in Express 4
It matches only the path "/*" literally
The app throws an error at startup about a missing parameter name
It matches every path but req.params is empty
questions.correctAnswer: The app throws an error at startup about a missing parameter name
questions.answer:
Why C: Express 5's path-to-regexp requires wildcards to have a name, so "*" alone is rejected when the route is created.

Why not A: The wildcard syntax changed in Express 5.

Why not B: The path is not treated as a literal string, it fails to parse.

Why not D: The route is never created, so it never matches.

Fix: app.get("/{*splat}", handler)

questions.question: A lessons router is mounted at "/courses/:courseId/lessons" and created with express.Router(). Inside it, what is req.params.courseId?
options: The course id from the URL
undefined
An empty string
The string ":courseId"
questions.correctAnswer: undefined
questions.answer:
Why B: A router does not see params defined on the path where it is mounted unless it is created with mergeParams: true.

Why not A: That is the result only with express.Router({ mergeParams: true }).

Why not C: Missing params are not filled with empty strings.

Why not D: Express never returns the pattern text as a value.

questions.question: Explain Express middleware with a real-life example, and name the main types of middleware.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Middleware is a function that sits between the request and the final route handler, like checkpoints at an airport: ticket check, security scan, passport control. Each one can let you through with next(), or stop you.

How it works: The five types:
Application-level: app.use(fn), runs for the whole app
Router-level: router.use(fn), runs only for that router's routes
Built-in: express.json(), express.urlencoded(), express.static()
Third-party: cors, helmet, morgan, cookie-parser
Error-handling: four arguments (err, req, res, next), runs only when an error happens

Example: A request to POST /api/quiz/submit passes cors, express.json(), a logger, then protect (checks the token), then the submit handler. If the token is missing, protect sends 401 and the handler never runs.

Common mistake: Thinking middleware is something special or complex. It is just a function with (req, res, next).

Interview tip: Give the airport example and then write a 3-line middleware on the whiteboard. Simple, correct and memorable beats long theory.

questions.question: How do you write a request logger middleware that logs the method, URL, status code and response time?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Record the start time, then listen for the response "finish" event. When it fires, the status code and duration are final, so you log them there.

How it works:
Start: const start = process.hrtime.bigint() or Date.now()
Wait: res.on('finish', ...) runs after the response is sent
Log: method, originalUrl, statusCode and milliseconds
Place it early: register it before the routes so it sees every request

Example: Logs like "GET /api/courses 200 34ms" and "POST /api/auth/login 401 120ms" show at a glance which endpoints are slow or failing.

Common mistake: Logging res.statusCode right at the start of the middleware. Nothing has been sent yet, so it always shows 200.

Interview tip: Mention that in production you would use morgan or a structured logger like pino-http, but writing one by hand proves you understand the request lifecycle.

questions.question: How does path matching work for app.use("/api", fn), and how is it different from router.use(fn)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: app.use with a path matches that path and everything under it, for any method. router.use(fn) without a path runs for every request that reaches that router.

How it works:
Prefix match: app.use('/api', fn) matches /api, /api/users and /api/a/b
Not a partial word: it does not match /apis or /api-docs
Stripped path: inside fn, req.path and req.url have /api removed, req.originalUrl keeps it
Router scope: router.use(protect) protects only the routes of that router

Example: In adminRoutes.js, router.use(protect, allowRoles('admin')) at the top protects every admin route in one line, while public routes in other files stay open.

Common mistake: Putting router.use(protect) in a router that is mounted at '/' or '/api'. It then runs for many unrelated requests that pass through that router, and public routes suddenly return 401.

Interview tip: Mention that mounting every protected router under its own prefix (like /api/admin) keeps the security boundary clear and easy to review.

questions.question: What do next("route") and next("router") do in Express?
questions.answer:
Short answer: next('route') skips the remaining callbacks of the current route and moves to the next matching route. next('router') leaves the current router completely and continues after it.

How it works:
next(): go to the next function in the same route or stack
next('route'): skip the rest of this route's middleware chain
next('router'): exit this router, continue in the parent
next(err): jump to error-handling middleware
Only works: next('route') only applies to app.METHOD and router.METHOD routes, not app.use

Example: A GET /courses/:id route first checks if the user is a premium member. If not, it calls next('route'), and a second GET /courses/:id route returns the free preview version of the course.

Common mistake: Passing any other string, like next('skip'). Express treats every value except 'route' and 'router' as an error, so the request ends up in the error handler.

Interview tip: Say these are rarely needed, and that clear separate routes or an if inside the handler are usually easier to read. Knowing them still shows deep Express knowledge.

questions.question: Which third-party middleware would you add to a new production Express API, and what does each one do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A common starter set is cors, helmet, express-rate-limit, morgan (or pino-http), compression and cookie-parser. Together they cover cross-origin access, security headers, abuse limits, logs, speed and cookies.

The ones you need:
cors: allows your frontend's domain to call the API from the browser
helmet: sets safe HTTP security headers in one line
express-rate-limit: limits requests per IP, stricter on login
morgan / pino-http: logs every request
compression: gzip or brotli for large JSON responses
cookie-parser: reads cookies into req.cookies

Example: A fresh MERN API adds these six in about ten lines of app.js. It instantly looks production-ready to a reviewer and blocks the most common basic attacks.

Common mistake: Adding packages without configuring them, like cors() with no options, which allows every website to call your API from a browser.

Interview tip: For each package, say why you need it and what you configured. "I set cors origin to CLIENT_URL and a 10-per-15-minutes limit on /auth/login" sounds like real experience.

questions.question: How do you pass data from one middleware to a later middleware or route handler?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Attach it to the req object (like req.user) or to res.locals. Both live only for the current request, so every later function in the chain can read it.

How it works:
req.user: the common place for the logged-in user, set by auth middleware
req.course: data preloaded by a param or loader middleware
res.locals: per-request storage, also visible to templates
Not globals: module variables are shared by all users and requests

Example: protect decodes the JWT and loads the user into req.user. allowRoles reads req.user.role. The controller uses req.user._id as the owner of the new course, never a userId from the request body.

Common mistake: Storing the current user in a variable at the top of a module, like let currentUser. With two users online at the same time, one request can overwrite the other's user.

Interview tip: If you use TypeScript, mention extending Express's Request type so req.user is typed. Remote teams often use TypeScript, and this question comes up.

questions.question: How do you apply an auth middleware to every route except a few public ones, like /login and /health?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The cleanest way is to mount public routes before the auth middleware, or put protected routes in their own router. A skip-list inside the middleware also works but is easier to get wrong.

How it works: Three options:
Order: app.use('/api/auth', authRoutes); then app.use('/api', protect); then protected routers
Separate routers: protected routers call router.use(protect) at their top
Skip list: if (PUBLIC_PATHS.includes(req.path)) return next(), inside protect

Example: A health check used by Render must work without a token. Registering /api/health before app.use('/api', protect) keeps it public with zero special-case code.

Common mistake: A skip list with exact strings. /api/auth/login/ (trailing slash) or /API/auth/login might not match the list, but routing still matches it, so the behaviour becomes inconsistent. Worse, a startsWith check can make a whole path tree public by accident.

Interview tip: Say you prefer "secure by default": everything is protected unless it is explicitly listed in a public router. New routes are then safe even if a developer forgets to add protect.

questions.question: req.body is undefined in your POST route even though the frontend sends data. List the possible causes and how to check each one.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Usually no body parser ran for that request. Either express.json() is missing or placed after the route, or the request's Content-Type does not match the parser, or the body is not what you think it is.

How it works: Checks in order:
Parser missing or late: app.use(express.json()) must come before the routes
Wrong Content-Type: express.json() only parses application/json requests
FormData from React: multipart data needs multer, not express.json()
HTML forms: application/x-www-form-urlencoded needs express.urlencoded()
Body on GET: many clients drop it, and APIs should not rely on it
Express 5: req.body stays undefined, not {}, when nothing was parsed

Example: A React fetch call sends JSON.stringify(data) but forgets headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }. The browser sends text/plain, express.json() skips it, and req.body is undefined.

Common mistake: Adding body-parser and express.json() together "just in case". It does not fix a wrong Content-Type and only hides the real cause.

Interview tip: Say you open the browser Network tab first to see the actual request headers and payload. Debugging from the real request beats guessing in code.

questions.question: How do you add a request ID to every request and include it in every log line, even deep inside service functions?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create or read an ID in an early middleware, return it in a response header, and store it in AsyncLocalStorage so any function called during that request can read it without passing it around.

How it works:
Create: crypto.randomUUID(), or reuse an incoming X-Request-Id header
Return: res.set('X-Request-Id', id) so users and support can quote it
Store: AsyncLocalStorage keeps a per-request context across awaits
Read: a logger helper adds the ID to every line automatically

Example: A user reports "payment failed" and sends a screenshot showing request ID 7f3c. You search the logs for 7f3c and see every line of that request, from the route to the database call, in seconds.

Common mistake: Storing the ID in a normal global variable. With many requests at once, logs mix IDs from different users and become useless.

Interview tip: Mention this is the base of distributed tracing. Tools like OpenTelemetry follow the same idea across several services. It is a strong talking point for remote backend roles.

questions.question: How would you write a simple in-memory cache middleware for GET routes, and what are its limits?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use the URL as the key. If a fresh copy exists, send it at once. If not, wrap res.json to save the body before sending. It is quick for one server but breaks down with many servers.

How it works:
Key: req.originalUrl, including the query string
Hit: send the stored body and skip the handler
Miss: patch res.json to store the body with an expiry time
Limits: memory grows, data is per process, restarts clear it, and every server has its own copy

Example: GET /api/languages changes maybe once a week but is called on every page load. A 60 second cache turns hundreds of database queries per minute into one.

Common mistake: Caching responses that depend on the user, like /api/me or anything behind auth, using only the URL as the key. User A's private data is then served to user B.

Interview tip: Say that for production with several instances you would move to Redis, and that you only cache public, read-heavy endpoints, clearing the cache when an admin updates the data.

questions.question: Inside a middleware, which call passes the request on to the next middleware or route?
options: res.continue()
next()
req.next()
return true
questions.correctAnswer: next()
questions.answer:
Why B: next is the third argument of a middleware. Calling it hands the request to the next matching function.

Why not A: res has no continue() method.

Why not C: The request object has no next() method.

Why not D: Express ignores return values of middleware. Only next() or a response moves things forward.

questions.question: A middleware is mounted with app.use("/api", fn). For a request to /api/users, what is req.path inside fn?
options: "/api/users"
"/api"
"/users"
"users"
questions.correctAnswer: "/users"
questions.answer:
Why C: app.use removes the mount path from req.path (and req.url) while the middleware runs, so "/api" is stripped.

Why not A: The full URL is still in req.originalUrl, not req.path.

Why not B: That is the mount path itself, not the remaining path.

Why not D: req.path always starts with a slash.

questions.question: What does calling next('route') inside a route's middleware do?
options: Skips the rest of this route's callbacks and goes to the next matching route
Restarts the current route from the beginning
Sends the request to the error handler
Ends the request with a 404
questions.correctAnswer: Skips the rest of this route's callbacks and goes to the next matching route
questions.answer:
Why A: next("route") jumps past the remaining functions of the current route and continues with the next route that matches.

Why not B: Express never restarts a route.

Why not C: "route" and "router" are the special strings that are not treated as errors. Other values do go to the error handler.

Why not D: A 404 comes only if no later route or middleware sends a response.

questions.question: What is the morgan package used for in an Express app?
options: Parsing cookies
Logging HTTP requests
Compressing responses
Setting security headers
questions.correctAnswer: Logging HTTP requests
questions.answer:
Why B: morgan is an HTTP request logger, printing lines like "GET /api 200 12ms".

Why not A: cookie-parser reads cookies.

Why not C: compression handles gzip and brotli.

Why not D: helmet sets security headers.

questions.question: A logger middleware prints res.statusCode on its first line, before calling next(). Why does it show 200 even for failed requests?
options: Express rewrites all status codes to 200 for logs
The middleware runs after the response is already sent
statusCode is only set for errors thrown with next(err)
Nothing has been sent yet, and 200 is just the default value
questions.correctAnswer: Nothing has been sent yet, and 200 is just the default value
questions.answer:
Why D: At that moment no handler has run, so res.statusCode still holds its starting value of 200.

Why not A: Express never changes status codes for logging.

Why not B: Middleware registered early runs before the route handler, not after the response.

Why not C: statusCode is set whenever any handler calls res.status(), not only for errors.

Fix: Log inside res.on("finish", ...), when the final status is known.

questions.question: The app uses express.json({ limit: "100kb" }) and a client sends a 2 MB JSON body. What happens?
options: Express keeps the first 100 KB and parses that part
The body parser rejects it with a 413 Payload Too Large error
req.body is set to an empty object and the route runs
Express increases the limit automatically for that request
questions.correctAnswer: The body parser rejects it with a 413 Payload Too Large error
questions.answer:
Why B: When the body is over the limit, the parser stops and passes an error with status 413 to the error handler.

Why not A: Express never cuts JSON into partial pieces. That would be invalid JSON.

Why not C: The route does not run, because an error is raised first.

Why not D: The limit is fixed by your configuration.

questions.question: What is the difference between res.send(), res.json() and res.end()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: res.json() always sends JSON. res.send() picks the type from what you give it (string as HTML, object as JSON, Buffer as binary). res.end() just closes the response, with no Express helpers.

How it works:
res.json(data): JSON.stringify plus Content-Type application/json
res.send(value): string becomes text/html, object becomes JSON, Buffer becomes octet-stream
res.end(): Node's raw method, used for empty replies or after streaming
res.sendStatus(204): sets the status and sends its text in one call

Example: An API should use res.json() everywhere, even for messages: res.json({ message: 'Saved' }). The React side can then always call response.json() safely.

Common mistake: Sending a plain string from an API, like res.send('Course deleted'). The frontend's response.json() fails with "Unexpected token C in JSON".

Interview tip: Say you standardize on res.status(code).json(body) in APIs so every response has the same shape and Content-Type.
questions.codeSnippet:
res.json({ message: 'Saved' }); // application/json res.send('

Hello

'); // text/html res.status(204).end(); // no body

questions.question: How do you set the status code and custom headers on an Express response?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Chain res.status(code) before sending, and use res.set(name, value) (or res.header) for headers. Both must happen before the body is sent.

How it works:
res.status(201).json(course): created
res.status(400).json({ errors }): bad input
res.set('Cache-Control', 'no-store'): any header
res.set(object): several headers at once
res.location('/api/courses/42'): sets the Location header

Example: After creating a course, a clean API replies 201 with the new course and a Location header pointing to it. Front-end developers and API tools like Postman read both.

Common mistake: Calling res.status(404) without sending anything. Setting the status alone does not finish the response, so the request hangs until timeout.

Interview tip: Mention that headers like X-Total-Count are a neat way to return pagination totals while keeping the JSON body a simple array.

questions.question: How do cookies work in Express, and how does a React app on another domain send them with each request?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The server sets a cookie with res.cookie(); the browser stores it and sends it back automatically. Read it with cookie-parser as req.cookies. Across domains, the frontend must use credentials: 'include' and CORS must allow credentials.

How it works:
res.cookie(name, value, options): sets it
httpOnly: JavaScript cannot read it
secure: only sent over HTTPS
sameSite: controls cross-site sending (Strict, Lax, None)
maxAge: lifetime in milliseconds
Frontend: fetch(url, { credentials: 'include' }) or axios withCredentials: true
Server: cors({ origin: CLIENT_URL, credentials: true })

Example: After login, the API sets an httpOnly token cookie. Every later request from the React app includes it, and the protect middleware reads req.cookies.token.

Common mistake: Forgetting credentials: 'include' in fetch. The cookie exists in the browser but is never sent, so the API keeps returning 401.

Interview tip: Mention that to clear a cookie with res.clearCookie(), you must pass the same path and domain options you used when setting it.

questions.question: How do you send files and downloads from Express safely?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use res.sendFile() to show a file and res.download() to make the browser save it. Always build the path from a safe folder and a name you control, never straight from user input.

How it works:
res.sendFile(absPath): sends with the right Content-Type
res.download(absPath, 'name.pdf'): adds Content-Disposition attachment
root option: res.sendFile(name, { root: folder }) refuses paths that escape the folder
Lookup: map an id to a stored file name in the database

Example: An admin downloads a backup with GET /api/admin/backups/:id. The handler finds the record, checks the admin role, and calls res.download() with the stored path and a friendly file name.

Common mistake: res.download('uploads/' + req.query.file). An attacker sends ?file=../.env and downloads your secrets. This is called path traversal.

Interview tip: Mention that for big files or many users, a signed link to cloud storage (S3, Cloudinary) is better, so file traffic does not go through your Node server.

questions.question: How do you read request headers, the client IP and the host in Express, and what changes behind a proxy like Render or Nginx?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use req.get('Header-Name') for headers, req.ip for the IP, and req.hostname or req.protocol for the host. Behind a proxy, these show the proxy's values unless you set app.set('trust proxy', 1).

How it works:
req.get('Authorization'): headers are case-insensitive
req.ip: client address, or the proxy's address without trust proxy
req.ips: full chain from X-Forwarded-For when trusted
req.protocol: http behind a TLS proxy unless trust proxy is set
req.secure: true only if the request is HTTPS (as Express sees it)

Example: On Render, without trust proxy every request seems to come from the same internal IP. The rate limiter then blocks all users together after a few hundred requests.

Common mistake: Setting trust proxy to true everywhere. Then anyone can fake X-Forwarded-For and pretend to be a different IP, which defeats rate limits.

Interview tip: Say you set trust proxy to the exact number of proxies in front of the app (often 1), and log req.ip once after deploy to confirm it shows real client IPs.

questions.question: How does res.redirect() work, and when do you use 301, 302, 307 and 308?
questions.answer:
Short answer: res.redirect(url) sends a 3xx status and a Location header, and the browser goes to the new URL. 302 is the default, meaning "temporarily somewhere else".

How it works:
301: moved permanently, browsers and search engines remember it
302: temporary (default), browsers usually change POST to GET
307: temporary, keeps the same method and body
308: permanent, keeps the same method and body

Example: An old URL /course/:id was renamed to /courses/:slug. A 301 redirect keeps old shared links and Google ranking working. After a login form POST, a 302 or 303 to /dashboard prevents the form being resubmitted on refresh.

Common mistake: Using 301 during testing. Browsers cache it strongly, so even after you remove the redirect, your browser keeps going to the old target until you clear the cache.

Interview tip: Mention that JSON APIs usually do not redirect. They return data or an error, and the React app decides where to navigate.

questions.question: How do you stream a large CSV export from Express without loading all records into memory?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read records with a database cursor and write each row to the response as you go. Memory stays small whether you export 1,000 or 1,000,000 rows.

How it works:
Headers first: Content-Type text/csv and Content-Disposition attachment
Cursor: Model.find().lean().cursor() gives one document at a time
Write: res.write(line) for each row, res.end() at the end
Backpressure: stream.pipeline handles slow clients for you
Errors: if the stream fails mid-way, you can only end the response

Example: An admin exports all quiz attempts. Loading 500,000 documents with find() needs hundreds of MB and can crash a 512 MB server. Streaming uses a few MB and the download starts immediately.

Common mistake: Building the whole CSV string in memory with join() and then res.send(). It works in testing with 50 rows and crashes in production.

Interview tip: Mention escaping values that contain commas, quotes or new lines, and adding a header row. These small details show you have built real exports.

questions.question: How do you send live updates from Express to the browser with Server-Sent Events (SSE), and when is it better than WebSockets?
questions.answer:
Short answer: SSE keeps one HTTP response open and the server writes "data:" lines into it whenever something happens. The browser reads them with EventSource. It is simpler than WebSockets when data only flows from server to client.

How it works:
Headers: Content-Type text/event-stream, Cache-Control no-cache
Message format: "data: {...}" followed by a blank line
Clients: keep a list of open res objects, remove one on req.on('close')
Browser: new EventSource('/api/notifications/stream')
Reconnect: built into EventSource automatically

Example: An admin dashboard shows "new user signed up" live. The signup route pushes an event to every connected admin, without polling every 5 seconds.

Common mistake: Forgetting to remove closed connections. The list grows forever, memory leaks, and writes to dead responses throw errors.

Interview tip: Say SSE is great for notifications, progress bars and live feeds. Use WebSockets (Socket.IO) for chat or games where the client also sends a lot. Also mention that compression middleware can buffer SSE, so disable it for that route.

questions.question: Login works on localhost, but after deploying the React app to Vercel and the API to Render, the auth cookie is never saved. Why, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The two sites are on different domains, so the cookie is cross-site. Browsers drop it unless it is sameSite 'none' and secure, CORS allows credentials, and Express knows it is behind HTTPS.

How it works: Checklist:
Cookie options: { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'none' }
trust proxy: app.set('trust proxy', 1), so Express sees the HTTPS request as secure
CORS: cors({ origin: 'https://yourapp.vercel.app', credentials: true }), not '*'
Frontend: credentials: 'include' on every fetch
Browser policy: some browsers block third-party cookies, so a custom domain like api.yourapp.com helps

Real example: Locally everything is "same-site" (localhost), so sameSite 'lax' works. In production the cookie gets a warning in DevTools and is silently ignored. Changing three options fixes it.

Common mistake: Switching to storing the JWT in localStorage to "fix" it. That works, but it gives up the XSS protection of httpOnly cookies.

Interview tip: Say you check DevTools: Application tab for the cookie and the Network tab's Set-Cookie warning icon. Remote interviewers love hearing exactly how you debug.

questions.question: What are ETags and 304 Not Modified responses in Express, and when can they cause confusing bugs?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express adds an ETag (a fingerprint of the body) to responses. If the browser sends the same ETag back in If-None-Match and nothing changed, Express replies 304 with no body, and the browser reuses its cached copy.

How it works:
Weak ETag: on by default for res.send and res.json
Request: browser sends If-None-Match: W/"8e-abc..."
Match: Express answers 304 Not Modified, empty body
Turn off: app.set('etag', false) or Cache-Control: no-store for private data

Example: The Network tab shows 304 for GET /api/courses. That is not an error: the data did not change, the response was smaller and faster, and the app shows the cached list.

Common mistake: Code that checks if (res.status !== 200) treat as error. With fetch the browser shows 200 to your code for a cached 304, but some HTTP clients or custom logic see the raw 304 and treat it as a failure.

Interview tip: Mention that for user-specific or fast-changing data you set Cache-Control: no-store, and for public data ETags plus max-age reduce load for free.

questions.question: What is the difference between GET and POST requests?
questions.answer:
Short answer: GET reads data: parameters go in the URL, it should not change anything on the server, and it can be cached and bookmarked. POST sends data in the request body to create something or trigger an action; it is not idempotent and is not cached by default.

How it works:
GET: data in the query string, like /api/questions?topic=closures; read with req.query
POST: data in the body (JSON or form); read with req.body after express.json()
Safe and idempotent: repeating a GET changes nothing; repeating a POST can create two records
Caching and history: browsers and CDNs cache GET; POST stays out of the URL, history and most logs

Example: GET /api/questions?topic=closures lists questions. POST /api/auth/login sends the email and password in the body.

Common mistake: Saying POST is "secure" because the data is not in the URL. Without HTTPS both are plain text on the network.

Interview tip: Mention the other methods: PUT replaces, PATCH updates part of a resource and DELETE removes; PUT and DELETE are idempotent too.

questions.question: Which line sends a JSON response with status 201 Created?
options: res.json(201, data)
res.send(data).status(201)
res.status(201).json(data)
res.created(data)
questions.correctAnswer: res.status(201).json(data)
questions.answer:
Why C: Set the status first, then send the body. status() returns res, so you can chain json().

Why not A: That old two-argument style was removed. In Express 5 it sends status 200 with the body 201.

Why not B: The response is already sent when status() is called, so the status cannot change.

Why not D: There is no res.created() method.

questions.question: What does res.sendStatus(404) send?
options: Only the status 404, with no body
Status 404 with the body "Not Found"
A JSON body { "status": 404 }
Status 200 with the body "404"
questions.correctAnswer: Status 404 with the body "Not Found"
questions.answer:
Why B: sendStatus sets the status and sends the standard status text as the body.

Why not A: It always sends the status text as a plain body.

Why not C: It does not build a JSON object.

Why not D: The given code is used as the status, not as the body of a 200.

questions.question: Which status code does res.redirect("/login") use by default?
questions.answer:
Why D: Express uses 302 Found unless you pass another code as the first argument.

Why not A: 301 is permanent and must be given explicitly: res.redirect(301, url).

Why not B: 307 keeps the method, and Express does not use it by default.

Why not C: 303 See Other is not the default either.

questions.question: An Express API runs on Render without app.set("trust proxy", ...). What does req.ip show?
options: The IP address of the proxy in front of the app, the same for most users
The real IP address of each user
Always 127.0.0.1
undefined
questions.correctAnswer: The IP address of the proxy in front of the app, the same for most users
questions.answer:
Why A: Without trust proxy, Express ignores X-Forwarded-For and reports the address that connected directly, which is the platform's proxy.

Why not B: The real IP is only read from X-Forwarded-For when you trust the proxy.

Why not C: The connection comes from the proxy, not from localhost.

Why not D: req.ip always has a value when there is a connection.

questions.question: A route calls res.download("uploads/" + req.query.name). What is the main risk?
options: Large files will always time out
The browser shows the file instead of downloading it
A user can request ?name=../.env and download files outside the uploads folder
File names with spaces cannot be downloaded
questions.correctAnswer: A user can request ?name=../.env and download files outside the uploads folder
questions.answer:
Why C: Joining user input into a path allows "../" to climb out of the folder. This is path traversal.

Why not A: Size affects speed, but it is not the main security risk here.

Why not B: res.download sets Content-Disposition attachment, so the browser saves it.

Why not D: Spaces work fine. The danger is unchecked path parts.

Fix: Look up the stored file name by id, or use the root option and reject names containing "..".

questions.question: The browser Network tab shows status 304 for GET /api/courses. What does it mean?
options: The server crashed and returned an empty response
The request was blocked by CORS
The user is not allowed to see the courses
The data matches the cached copy (same ETag), so the browser reuses its cached response
questions.correctAnswer: The data matches the cached copy (same ETag), so the browser reuses its cached response
questions.answer:
Why D: The browser sent If-None-Match with the old ETag, Express found the body unchanged and answered 304 with no body.

Why not A: A crash gives a 5xx status or a network error, not 304.

Why not B: CORS problems show as a blocked or failed request, not a 304.

Why not C: Permission problems use 401 or 403.

questions.question: What does Express do by default when a route throws an error and you have not written any error handler?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express's built-in final handler catches it, logs it, and replies with status 500 (or err.status if set) and an HTML error page. In development the page includes the stack trace; in production (NODE_ENV=production) it shows only the status text.

How it works:
Status: err.status or err.statusCode if it is between 400 and 599, otherwise 500
Body: an HTML page, not JSON
Stack trace: shown unless NODE_ENV is production
Server: keeps running, only that request fails

Example: A React app calls an API route that throws. The frontend gets an HTML page instead of JSON, and response.json() fails with "Unexpected token <", which hides the real error.

Common mistake: Forgetting to set NODE_ENV=production on the server. The default handler then sends stack traces with file paths and code details to every user.

Interview tip: Say every API should have its own error middleware that returns consistent JSON, and that the default handler is only a safety net.

questions.question: How do you add a "route not found" handler in Express, and why must it come after all other routes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Add a middleware with no path at the very end, after all routers. If a request reaches it, no route matched, so it returns 404 or passes a 404 error to the error handler.

How it works:
Position: after every app.use(router) and app.get()
Option 1: respond directly, res.status(404).json(...)
Option 2: create an error with status 404 and call next(err), so your error handler formats it
Then: the error handler is registered last of all

Example: A typo in the frontend calls /api/couses. The API answers { "message": "Route /api/couses not found" } in JSON, and the developer spots the typo at once.

Common mistake: Placing the 404 handler above a router. Everything below it is unreachable and every route seems "not found".

Interview tip: Mention including the method and URL in the message, and that this handler is different from "resource not found" (a valid route but the course id does not exist), which the controller handles itself.

questions.question: How do you turn Mongoose errors like ValidationError, CastError and duplicate key (11000) into clean API responses?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Check the error's name or code in your central error handler and map each one to the right status and a friendly message, before the generic 500 fallback.

How it works:
ValidationError: 400, list err.errors fields with their messages
CastError: 400, "Invalid id" (for example findById("abc"))
code 11000: 409 Conflict, read err.keyValue to say which field is taken
Others: 500 with a generic message, full details only in logs

Example: Signing up with an existing email returns 409 { "message": "email already exists", "field": "email" }. The React form shows the message right under the email input.

Common mistake: Returning err.message from Mongoose directly. Users see things like "E11000 duplicate key error collection: test.users index: email_1", which is confusing and exposes database details.

Interview tip: Say this mapping lives in one place, so every controller can simply throw or await and never needs its own try/catch for database errors.

questions.question: Why should you not send err.stack or raw error messages to clients in production?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Raw errors leak internal details that help attackers and confuse users. Send a safe, short message to the client and keep the full error in your server logs.

How it works: What raw errors can reveal:
File paths: /opt/render/project/src/controllers/userController.js
Libraries and versions: makes it easier to find known exploits
Database details: collection names, index names and queries
Secrets: sometimes a failed connection string or token appears in the message

Example: A 500 error on the live site shows "MongoServerError: bad auth: authentication failed" with the cluster host name. Now an attacker knows your database provider and host.

Common mistake: Writing one handler that does res.json({ error: err }) everywhere. In production it sends everything, and the stack can include code snippets.

Interview tip: Mention returning a request ID with each 500 response. Support can then find the full error in the logs, without users ever seeing internal details.

questions.question: Express 5 catches errors from async route handlers. Which errors does it still NOT catch, and how do you handle them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Express catches errors thrown in the handler or from a rejected promise it returns. It does not catch errors thrown later inside callbacks, timers or event listeners, because those run outside the handler's promise.

How it works: Not caught automatically:
Old callbacks: fs.readFile(path, (err) => { throw err })
Timers: setTimeout(() => { throw ... })
Events: stream.on('error', ...) and emitter events
Fire-and-forget promises: sendEmail() without await
Fix: promisify callbacks, await everything, or call next(err) inside the callback

Example: A route reads a file with a callback and does if (err) throw err. The file is missing, the throw happens outside Express, and the whole Node process crashes with an uncaught exception.

Common mistake: Thinking "Express 5 handles async errors" means no error can crash the server anymore.

Interview tip: Say you prefer promise APIs (fs/promises, stream/promises pipeline) so every error flows into one place, and you keep a process-level handler only as a last safety net.

questions.question: In Express 5, what is the difference between throwing an error and calling next(err), and when do you still need next(err)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Inside a handler or async middleware, throw and next(err) both reach the error handler. You still need next(err) in callback-style code and in places where you must not stop the current function abruptly.

How it works:
throw: simple in async functions, Express catches the rejected promise
next(err): works everywhere, including callbacks and Express 4
return next(err): use return so code after it does not run
Sync middleware: a plain throw is caught too

Example: In multer's callback upload(req, res, (err) => { ... }), a throw would escape Express. Calling next(err) there sends the upload error to your central handler.

Common mistake: Calling next(err) and then continuing, like next(err); res.json(data). Both the error handler and the handler try to respond, giving "headers already sent".

Interview tip: Say you choose one style per project for clarity, for example "throw custom errors in async code, next(err) only in callbacks".

questions.question: Some API requests hang forever: no response, no error in the logs. How do you find the cause?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A hanging request means some code path never sends a response and never calls next(). Find which middleware or branch it stops in by logging, then fix the missing response.

How it works: Usual causes:
Middleware without next(): an if branch returns without responding
Unhandled branch: if (a) res.json(); else if (b) res.json(); and no final else
Promise never resolving: a wrapped callback that never calls resolve
Awaiting nothing: a database call with no connection (Mongoose buffers queries)
Debug: add a response-time logger and a timeout middleware to see where it stops

Example: The protect middleware does if (!token) return; instead of return res.status(401).json(...). Every logged-out request hangs until the browser gives up after minutes.

Common mistake: Increasing timeouts on the client or the host. The request still never finishes, it just fails later.

Interview tip: Mention that a request timeout middleware (for example 30 seconds, then 503) and alerts on long requests turn silent hangs into visible errors.

questions.question: How would you design error responses with machine-readable error codes so a React frontend can show the right message?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Return a stable code (like EMAIL_TAKEN) together with a human message and, for forms, per-field errors. The frontend switches on the code, not on the text, so messages can change or be translated safely.

How it works: A response shape that works well:
status: the HTTP status, for the type of problem
code: a fixed string like VALIDATION_FAILED or PLAN_LIMIT_REACHED
message: readable text for a toast
errors: { field: message } for inline form errors
AppError class: carries status and code from anywhere in the code

Example: When a free user hits the daily limit, the API returns 403 with code FREE_LIMIT_REACHED. The React app sees that code and opens the "Upgrade" dialog instead of a generic error toast.

Common mistake: Making the frontend check message text, like if (msg.includes('limit')). A small wording change on the server breaks the UI.

Interview tip: Mention documenting the error codes in your API docs. Remote teams with separate frontend and backend developers work much faster with a written error contract.

questions.question: A route starts a background task (like sending a welcome email) without waiting for it. How do you stop its errors from crashing the server?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An unawaited promise that rejects is an unhandled rejection, and modern Node exits the process on it. Always attach a .catch() that logs the error, or hand the job to a queue.

How it works:
Fire-and-forget: sendWelcomeEmail(user).catch(logError)
Why: the request has already finished, so the error handler cannot help
Node 15+: unhandled rejections crash the process by default
Better: a job queue (BullMQ with Redis) with retries and a failed-jobs list

Example: The email provider is down for 10 minutes. Without .catch(), the first failed email crashes the API and every user sees 502 until it restarts. With .catch(), signups keep working and the failures are logged for a retry.

Common mistake: Adding await to make it safe. Now the user waits for the email provider on every signup, and a slow provider makes signup slow.

Interview tip: Say you also add process.on('unhandledRejection') logging as a last line of defence, but you never rely on it for normal flow.

questions.question: What should your error-handling middleware do if an error happens after the response has already started sending?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Check res.headersSent. If headers are already sent, you cannot send a new status or JSON, so pass the error to Express's default handler with next(err), which closes the connection.

How it works:
headersSent false: send your normal JSON error
headersSent true: return next(err), do not call res.status() or res.json()
Default handler: ends the broken response and logs the error
Typical cases: streaming a file or CSV fails mid-way

Example: A CSV export has written 3 MB when the database connection drops. Your handler sees headersSent is true and delegates. The download ends early, and the error is logged instead of a second "headers already sent" crash.

Common mistake: Always calling res.status(500).json() in the error handler. During streaming it throws its own error, which hides the original problem in the logs.

Interview tip: Mention that this is one of the few cases where calling next(err) from inside an error handler is correct, and that Express's docs recommend exactly this check.

questions.question: Where should you register your error-handling middleware?
options: At the top of app.js, before any other middleware
Right after express.json()
After all routes and other middleware
Inside each route handler
questions.correctAnswer: After all routes and other middleware
questions.answer:
Why C: Express runs middleware in order, so the error handler must come last to receive errors from everything above it.

Why not A: Registered first, it would never see errors from routes added after it.

Why not B: Routes added after that point would not be covered.

Why not D: Error middleware is registered with app.use, not inside handlers.

questions.question: Your error handler does res.status(err.status || 500). What status does a Mongoose CastError from User.findById("abc") get?
options: 500, because a CastError has no status property
400, Mongoose sets it automatically
404, because no user was found
422, the standard for cast errors
questions.correctAnswer: 500, because a CastError has no status property
questions.answer:
Why A: Mongoose errors do not carry an HTTP status, so the fallback 500 is used.

Why not B: Mongoose knows nothing about HTTP and never sets status codes.

Why not C: findById("abc") fails before searching, so it is not a "not found" result.

Why not D: No library sets 422 for you. You would have to map it yourself.

Fix: Map err.name === "CastError" to 400 in the error handler.

questions.question: The 404 handler app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json(...)) is placed above app.use("/api", apiRouter). What happens?
options: Only unknown routes get 404
Express moves the 404 handler to the end automatically
API routes still work because routers have priority
Every request to the API returns 404
questions.correctAnswer: Every request to the API returns 404
questions.answer:
Why D: The 404 middleware matches every request and sends a response, so the request never reaches the router below it.

Why not A: The handler does not know which routes exist below it. It answers everything.

Why not B: Express keeps the exact order you register.

Why not C: Routers have no special priority, order decides.

questions.question: Which MongoDB error code means a unique index was violated, for example a duplicate email?
options: E_DUP
questions.answer:
Why B: MongoDB reports duplicate keys with error code 11000, and err.keyValue shows the duplicated field.

Why not A: 404 is an HTTP status, not a MongoDB error code.

Why not C: 500 is an HTTP status for server errors.

Why not D: There is no E_DUP code. The message text starts with E11000, but the code is the number 11000.

questions.question: In Express 5, a route runs fs.readFile(p, (err, data) => { if (err) throw err; res.send(data); }) and the file is missing. What happens?
options: Express catches it and sends a 500 response
The error is ignored and the request hangs
The throw happens outside Express, causing an uncaught exception that crashes the process
Express retries the read once
questions.correctAnswer: The throw happens outside Express, causing an uncaught exception that crashes the process
questions.answer:
Why C: The callback runs later, outside the handler's call stack and promise, so Express cannot catch it and Node treats it as uncaught.

Why not A: Express 5 only catches errors thrown synchronously in the handler or from a rejected promise it returns.

Why not B: An uncaught exception is not ignored, it stops the process.

Why not D: Express never retries file reads.

Fix: Use fs/promises with await, or call next(err) inside the callback.

questions.question: An error happens while a large file is half sent. What should the error handler do?
options: Call res.status(500).json({ message })
Call next(err) so Express's default handler closes the connection
Restart the download from the beginning
Ignore the error, since the user already got part of the file
questions.correctAnswer: Call next(err) so Express's default handler closes the connection
questions.answer:
Why B: Headers are already sent, so a new status and body are impossible. Delegating lets Express end the response and log the error.

Why not A: This throws "Cannot set headers after they are sent" and hides the real error.

Why not C: Express cannot restart a response that is already in progress.

Why not D: Ignoring it leaves the connection hanging and the error unlogged.

questions.question: Why must an Express API validate input on the server even when the React form already validates it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Frontend validation is for user experience, server validation is for safety. Anyone can skip your form and send any request with Postman, curl or the browser console.

How it works:
Frontend checks: quick feedback, can be bypassed in seconds
Server checks: the only checks an attacker cannot skip
Other clients: mobile apps, scripts and old app versions also call the API
Database rules: the last line of defence, not the first

Example: The signup form requires a password of 8+ characters. A user edits the request in DevTools and sends a 1 character password, or a role field the form never shows. Only the server can reject that.

Common mistake: Copying the frontend rules to the server "later" and forgetting. The API then accepts empty titles, negative prices and huge strings.
