Interview tip: Say "Never trust the client". Then mention you validate type, length, format and allowed values, and you reject unknown fields. That is what interviewers want to hear.

questions.question: How do you use express-validator to validate a request body and return the errors?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Add validation chains like body('email').isEmail() to the route, then call validationResult(req) in a small middleware. If there are errors, return 400 with them; if not, call next().

How it works:
Chains: body(), param(), query() with checks like isLength, isInt, isIn
Sanitizers: trim(), toLowerCase(), toInt() clean the value
Messages: withMessage('Email is not valid')
Collect: validationResult(req).array() gives every error
Reuse: one validate middleware for all routes

Example: The register route checks name (2 to 50 characters), email (valid, lowercased) and password (8+ characters). A bad request gets 400 with the list of problems, and the controller code stays clean.

Common mistake: Writing the chains but never checking validationResult. The checks run, collect errors, and then the controller saves the bad data anyway.

Interview tip: Mention matchedData(req), which returns only the validated fields, so unexpected fields like role never reach your database.

questions.question: How do schema validators like zod or Joi work in an Express API, and how do they compare to express-validator?
questions.answer:
Short answer: You describe the whole expected object once as a schema, then check req.body against it in one middleware. The result is clean, typed data with unknown fields removed.

How it works:
Schema: z.object({ title: z.string().min(3), price: z.number().min(0) })
Check: schema.safeParse(req.body) returns success and data, or the errors
Unknown keys: zod strips them by default, Joi can strip with stripUnknown
Reuse: the same schema can validate on the React side too

Example: A createCourse schema is shared between the React form (with react-hook-form) and the Express route. Both sides now agree on the rules, with no duplicated checks.

Common mistake: Validating and then saving req.body instead of the parsed result. The cleaned and stripped data is thrown away and extra fields still go to the database.

Interview tip: Say express-validator fits route-by-route checks, while zod shines with TypeScript because it creates types from the schema. Teams often choose zod for new projects.

questions.question: What is the difference between validation and sanitization, and why do you need both?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Validation checks if data is acceptable and rejects it if not. Sanitization cleans or transforms data into a safe, standard form. You sanitize to normalize, then validate the clean result.

How it works:
Validation: isEmail, isLength, isIn(['easy', 'medium', 'hard'])
Sanitization: trim, toLowerCase, toInt, escape
Order: trim first, then check the length, or "   " passes as 3 characters
Escaping HTML: only when the value will be shown as HTML

Example: A user signs up as " Ali@Gmail.COM ". Sanitizing gives "ali@gmail.com", so a later login with "ali@gmail.com" finds the account and the unique email index really works.

Common mistake: Escaping every field "for security" before saving. Names like O'Brien become O'Brien in the database, and React then shows the escaped text because it already escapes output itself.

Interview tip: Say you normalize data on input and escape on output, depending on where it is shown (HTML, SQL, shell). That shows a mature understanding of XSS prevention.

questions.question: How do you accept a file upload in Express with multer, and what does req.file contain?
questions.answer:
Short answer: multer parses multipart/form-data requests. Add upload.single('avatar') to the route, and the file details appear in req.file while the text fields appear in req.body.

How it works:
Storage: diskStorage (save to a folder) or memoryStorage (keep a Buffer)
single('field'): one file, req.file
array('field', 5): many files of one field, req.files
req.file: fieldname, originalname, mimetype, size, and path or buffer
Frontend: send a FormData object, do not set Content-Type yourself

Example: A profile page uploads an avatar. The route uses upload.single('avatar'), saves the file name to the user, and returns the new image URL.

Common mistake: Setting headers: { 'Content-Type': 'multipart/form-data' } by hand in fetch or axios. The browser then cannot add the boundary value, and multer fails to read the body.

Interview tip: Mention that you always set limits (file size, number of files) in the multer options, which is the first protection against abuse.

questions.question: How do you validate MongoDB ObjectIds and enum values coming from requests in an Express API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Check ids with mongoose.isValidObjectId() (or a validator rule) and enums with a fixed list of allowed values, before any database query. Invalid input should get 400, not a 500 from a CastError.

How it works:
Ids: isValidObjectId(id), or express-validator param('id').isMongoId()
Enums: isIn(['easy', 'medium', 'hard']) or z.enum([...])
Share lists: export allowed values from one constants file used by the schema and the validator
Arrays of ids: check every item, not just the first one

Example: GET /api/questions?difficulty=expert returns 400 "difficulty must be easy, medium or hard" instead of silently returning an empty list that confuses the frontend developer.

Common mistake: Writing the allowed values in three places (Mongoose schema, validator, React dropdown). When you add "expert", one place is forgotten and requests fail strangely.

Interview tip: Mention that clear 400 errors with the allowed values make an API self-explaining, which saves frontend developers a lot of time in remote teams.

questions.question: How do you make file uploads in Express secure?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Limit size and count, accept only the types you need (checked by content, not only by the file name), give files random names, store them outside your code folder (or in cloud storage), and never run or trust uploaded content.

How it works:
Limits: multer limits fileSize and files
Type check: fileFilter on mimetype, plus checking the real bytes with a library like file-type
Random names: crypto.randomUUID() plus a safe extension, never originalname
Location: cloud storage, or a folder that is served as static files only
Images: re-encode with sharp, which also removes hidden metadata
Access: private files need an auth check or signed URLs

Example: Someone uploads "photo.jpg" that is really an HTML page with a script. If you keep the name and serve it as HTML, visitors run the attacker's script on your domain.

Common mistake: Trusting file.mimetype alone. It comes from the client, so it can be faked as easily as the file name.

Interview tip: Mention scanning uploads with antivirus or a cloud service for public apps, and setting Content-Disposition attachment for files users download.

questions.question: Where should an Express app on Render or Railway store uploaded files in production, and why not just the local uploads folder?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use object storage like Cloudinary, AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2. Platform disks are usually ephemeral: files saved locally disappear on every deploy or restart, and they are not shared between instances.

How it works:
Ephemeral disk: wiped on redeploy, restart or scaling
Multiple instances: a file saved on server A is missing on server B
Object storage: durable, cheap, has a CDN, scales by itself
Flow 1: multer memoryStorage, then upload the buffer to storage
Flow 2: the API gives the browser a presigned URL, and the browser uploads directly

Real example: A student's portfolio app saves profile photos to /uploads on Render's free tier. After the next git push, every photo shows a broken image. Moving to Cloudinary fixes it, and images load faster through its CDN.

Common mistake: Storing images as Base64 inside MongoDB documents to avoid this. Documents get huge, queries slow down and you approach the 16 MB limit.

Interview tip: Say presigned uploads are best for large files, because the file never passes through your Node server, which saves bandwidth and memory.

questions.question: How do you validate query parameters for a list endpoint so users cannot abuse it with values like limit=100000 or sort=password?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Treat query values as untrusted strings. Convert them to numbers with safe ranges, cap the page size, and only allow sort and filter fields from a whitelist.

How it works:
page: integer, at least 1, default 1
limit: integer between 1 and 50, default 20
sort: one of ['createdAt', '-createdAt', 'title']
filters: only known keys, cast to the right type
Unknown keys: ignore them or reject with 400

Example: A scraper calls /api/questions?limit=100000. Without a cap the API loads every question into memory and slows down for everyone. With the cap, it gets 50 at most.

Common mistake: Building the sort from user input, like .sort(req.query.sort). Sorting by a field like password hash or an unindexed field can leak information or force slow in-memory sorts.

Interview tip: Mention returning the effective values (page, limit, total) in the response, so clients know the cap was applied and can paginate correctly.

questions.question: How do you return validation errors so a React form can show each message next to the right input?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Return 400 with an errors object keyed by field name, like { email: 'Email is already used', password: 'At least 8 characters' }. The form maps each key to its input.

How it works:
Shape: { code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED', message: 'Please fix the errors', errors: { field: message } }
Same shape: for validator errors, Mongoose ValidationError and duplicate key 409s
Nested fields: use dot paths like "address.city"
React: react-hook-form setError(field, { message }) for each key

Example: A signup form submits. The API returns errors for email and password at once, and both messages appear under their inputs, instead of one generic toast the user has to guess from.

Common mistake: Returning only the first error. The user fixes one field, submits again, gets the next error, and gets frustrated after three rounds.

Interview tip: Say you agree on this error shape with the frontend team at the start of a project. In take-home tasks, showing field-level errors is a small detail that makes your work stand out.

questions.question: Which package is commonly used to handle multipart/form-data file uploads in Express?
options: body-parser
multer
cors
express.json()
questions.correctAnswer: multer
questions.answer:
Why B: multer is built for multipart/form-data and gives you req.file and req.files.

Why not A: body-parser handles JSON and URL-encoded bodies, not multipart.

Why not C: cors controls cross-origin access, it does not parse bodies.

Why not D: express.json() only parses application/json bodies.

questions.question: A React app sends a FormData with a "title" field and an image. The route only has express.json(). What is req.body?
options: { title: "..." } with the image ignored
{ title: "...", image: "..." }
A string containing the raw form data
Not parsed, because express.json() does not read multipart/form-data
questions.correctAnswer: Not parsed, because express.json() does not read multipart/form-data
questions.answer:
Why D: express.json() only parses JSON. A multipart body is skipped, so neither the text fields nor the file are parsed.

Why not A: The text fields are inside the same multipart body, so they are not parsed either.

Why not B: Nothing reads the multipart body, so no fields appear.

Why not C: Express does not turn unknown bodies into strings.

Fix: Add multer, for example upload.single("image"), to that route.

questions.question: The route uses upload.single("avatar"), but the frontend appends the file as formData.append("image", file). What happens?
options: multer rejects it with a MulterError for an unexpected field
multer renames the field to avatar automatically
The file is saved, and req.file is set normally
req.file is undefined but no error is raised
questions.correctAnswer: multer rejects it with a MulterError for an unexpected field
questions.answer:
Why A: multer only accepts the file field you named. A file under any other field name raises a MulterError with code LIMIT_UNEXPECTED_FILE.

Why not B: multer never renames fields.

Why not C: The field name does not match, so the file is not accepted.

Why not D: multer reports an error for unexpected file fields rather than silently ignoring them.

questions.question: Why is checking only the file extension of an upload, like ".jpg", not enough?
options: Extensions are always lowercase, so checks fail
Browsers remove extensions before uploading
Anyone can rename a dangerous file to end with .jpg
multer deletes the extension before you can check it
questions.correctAnswer: Anyone can rename a dangerous file to end with .jpg
questions.answer:
Why C: The name is chosen by the user. An HTML or script file renamed to photo.jpg still has dangerous content.

Why not A: Extensions can be any case, and that is a minor detail, not the real problem.

Why not B: Browsers send the original file name, including the extension.

Why not D: multer keeps originalname with its extension.

questions.question: With zod, what is the difference between schema.parse(data) and schema.safeParse(data)?
options: parse validates types only, safeParse also checks lengths
parse throws a ZodError on invalid data, safeParse returns { success, data or error } without throwing
safeParse also escapes HTML in strings
There is no difference, safeParse is an old alias
questions.correctAnswer: parse throws a ZodError on invalid data, safeParse returns { success, data or error } without throwing
questions.answer:
Why B: parse throws when data is invalid, while safeParse returns a result object you check with success.

Why not A: Both run all the same checks.

Why not C: zod does not escape HTML.

Why not D: They behave differently: one throws, one returns.

questions.question: An Express app on a free cloud host saves uploads to a local "uploads" folder. What usually happens after the next deploy?
options: The files are moved to the new version automatically
Uploads become read-only but stay available
The host converts them into a database backup
The uploaded files are gone, because the disk is reset on each deploy or restart
questions.correctAnswer: The uploaded files are gone, because the disk is reset on each deploy or restart
questions.answer:
Why D: Most platforms give apps an ephemeral filesystem. Each deploy or restart starts from a fresh copy of your code.

Why not A: Nothing copies runtime files between deploys.

Why not B: They are not kept at all, read-only or otherwise.

Why not C: Hosts do not turn files into database backups.

Fix: Store uploads in object storage like Cloudinary, S3 or R2, or attach a persistent disk.

questions.question: Walk through the full signup and login flow in an Express + MongoDB app.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Signup validates input, hashes the password with bcrypt and saves the user. Login finds the user by email, compares the password with bcrypt.compare, and issues a token (JWT or session). Protected routes then check that token.

How it works:
Signup: validate, lowercase the email, hash with bcrypt (cost 10 to 12), save, return 201
Login: find by email, bcrypt.compare, same error for wrong email or wrong password
Token: jwt.sign({ id }, secret, { expiresIn: '1d' }), sent as httpOnly cookie or in the JSON body
Protect: middleware verifies the token and loads req.user
Logout: clear the cookie or delete the token on the client

Example: Ayesha signs up, logs in and opens /dashboard. React calls GET /api/auth/me, the protect middleware verifies her token, and the API returns her profile without the password field.

Common mistake: Returning the user document straight from the database after login, including the password hash. Always remove it with select('-password') or toJSON.

Interview tip: Draw the flow as 4 boxes (signup, login, token, protect). A clear diagram plus "same error message for both cases" makes a strong first impression.

questions.question: Roles are not enough: a teacher may edit only their own courses. How do you implement ownership checks in Express?
questions.answer:
Short answer: After authentication, load the resource and compare its owner with req.user. Allow the action if the user owns it (or is an admin), otherwise return 403. Better still, put the owner into the query itself.

How it works:
Role check: is this user a teacher at all
Ownership check: course.owner equals req.user._id
Query style: Course.findOne({ _id: id, owner: req.user._id }) returns null for other people's courses
Admin override: admins skip the owner condition

Example: Teacher A sends PATCH /api/courses/B-course-id by changing the id in the URL. With an ownership check the API returns 404 (or 403), so A cannot change B's course.

Common mistake: Checking only the role. Any teacher can then edit any course by guessing or copying ids. This is called IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) and is one of the most common API security bugs.

Interview tip: Mention returning 404 instead of 403 for private resources, so attackers cannot even confirm that a resource exists.

questions.question: How do you implement a secure "forgot password" flow in Express?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create a random token, store only its hash with a short expiry, email a link with the plain token, and on reset compare the hash, check expiry, set the new password and delete the token so it works only once.

How it works:
Token: crypto.randomBytes(32).toString('hex')
Store: sha256 hash of the token plus expires (for example 30 minutes)
Response: always "If that email exists, we sent a link", even for unknown emails
Reset: hash the token from the link, find a user with that hash and expires > now
After reset: hash the new password, clear the token, optionally log out other sessions

Example: A user clicks the reset link 2 hours later. The token has expired, so the API says "Link expired, request a new one". The same link cannot be reused after a successful reset either.

Common mistake: Storing the plain token in the database. Anyone who sees the database (a leaked backup, a curious developer) can reset any account.

Interview tip: Mention rate-limiting the forgot-password route, so attackers cannot use it to spam people's inboxes or to test which emails exist.

questions.question: How do you add email verification after signup in an Express app?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Save the user as unverified, send a link with a one-time token, and mark the user verified when the link is opened. Block or limit features until the email is verified.

How it works:
Signup: emailVerified false, hashed token, expiry of 24 hours
Email: link to /verify-email?token=...
Verify route: hash the token, find the user, set emailVerified true, clear the token
Resend: a rate-limited "send again" endpoint
Guard: a middleware that returns 403 with code EMAIL_NOT_VERIFIED for certain routes

Example: A user signs up with a typo in their email. They never get the link, and the app shows "Check your email or resend the link". Without verification, password resets would go to a stranger's inbox later.

Common mistake: Making the verify link work with a GET that changes data and is opened by email scanners first. Some corporate email systems open links automatically, so a confirmation page with a button (POST) is safer.

Interview tip: Mention that services like Brevo, Resend or SendGrid send these emails, and that the email send should not block the signup response.

questions.question: What should you put inside a JWT payload, and what should you never put there?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Keep it small: a user id and maybe a role and a token version. Never put passwords, secrets or private personal data in it, because anyone holding the token can decode and read it.

How it works:
Good: sub or id, role, tokenVersion, plus iat and exp (added by the library)
Never: password or its hash, API keys, card data, address, phone
Signed, not encrypted: the signature stops changes, but not reading
Size: the token is sent with every request, so big payloads slow things down

Example: Paste any JWT into a decoder site and the payload is visible in plain text. If it held { email, phone, address }, every browser extension or log that sees the token could read them.

Common mistake: Trusting the role in the token for too long. If an admin is demoted, a 30-day token still says "admin" until it expires.

Interview tip: Say you keep access tokens short-lived (15 minutes to a day) and load fresh user data from the database in protect, so permission changes take effect quickly.

questions.question: Why should a login endpoint answer "Invalid email or password" instead of "Email not found" or "Wrong password"?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Separate messages tell an attacker which emails have accounts. That is called user enumeration, and it makes targeted password guessing and phishing much easier.

How it works:
Same message: for unknown email and wrong password
Same status: 401 in both cases
Same timing: still run a bcrypt compare when the user is missing, so response time does not give it away
Same idea: forgot-password and signup should not reveal it either where possible

Example: An attacker has a list of 10,000 leaked emails. With "Email not found" they learn exactly which ones use your site, then try common passwords only on those accounts.

Common mistake: Hiding it at login but returning "This email is not registered" on the forgot-password page. The leak just moves to another endpoint.

Interview tip: Mention the trade-off: signup must say "email already used" for good UX. You reduce the risk there with rate limits and CAPTCHA instead.

questions.question: How would you add "Sign in with Google" to an Express + React app?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use Google's OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect. The simplest safe flow: the React app gets a Google ID token, sends it to your API, the API verifies it with Google's library, then finds or creates the user and issues your own session or JWT.

How it works:
Frontend: Google Identity Services button returns a credential (ID token)
Backend: google-auth-library verifyIdToken with your client ID as audience
Checks: signature, audience, expiry and email_verified
User: find by googleId, or link to an existing account with the same verified email
Session: then issue your normal app token, same as password login

Example: A student clicks "Continue with Google", and the API receives the ID token, verifies it, creates the account with name and avatar from Google, and logs them in. No password to forget.

Common mistake: Trusting the email sent from the frontend without verifying the token on the server. Anyone could then log in as any email address.

Interview tip: Mention Passport.js as the classic alternative with a server-side redirect flow, and that you keep OAuth users and password users in the same users collection with an authProvider field.

questions.question: Beyond a simple IP rate limit, how do you protect a login route from brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Combine limits per IP and per account, slow down repeated failures, add CAPTCHA after a few failures, alert on unusual activity, and offer 2FA. Attackers rotate IPs, so per-IP limits alone are not enough.

How it works:
Per IP: for example 10 attempts per 15 minutes
Per account: count failures on the email, add a short lock or delay after 5
CAPTCHA: shown after repeated failures, not on the first try
Breached passwords: reject known leaked passwords at signup (Have I Been Pwned API)
Monitoring: log failed logins and alert on spikes
2FA: stops attackers even when they have the right password

Example: A botnet tries leaked email and password pairs from 5,000 IPs, 2 tries each. IP limits never trigger, but the per-account counter and the CAPTCHA stop it.

Common mistake: Locking accounts permanently after 5 failures. Attackers can then lock out real users on purpose, which is a denial of service.

Interview tip: Use the term "credential stuffing" and explain how it differs from brute force. It shows you follow real-world security, which remote companies care about.

questions.question: How do you handle an expired JWT smoothly between React and Express so the user is not suddenly logged out?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a short-lived access token and a longer-lived refresh token in an httpOnly cookie. When an API call returns 401 with a "token expired" code, the frontend calls /auth/refresh once, gets a new access token, and retries the original request.

How it works:
Server: protect returns 401 with code TOKEN_EXPIRED for an expired token
Refresh route: checks the refresh cookie and returns a new access token
Client: an axios interceptor catches that 401, refreshes, retries
Single flight: if 5 requests fail together, refresh only once and queue the rest
Logout: if refresh also fails, clear state and go to the login page

Example: A student is in the middle of a 20-minute quiz when the 15-minute access token expires. The submit call gets 401, the interceptor refreshes silently, and the quiz is submitted without them noticing.

Common mistake: Refreshing on every 401, including "wrong password" or "no permission". That can create infinite refresh loops.

Interview tip: Mention rotating the refresh token on every use and detecting reuse of an old one, which signals theft. This detail impresses senior interviewers.

questions.question: How would you add two-factor authentication (2FA) with an authenticator app to an Express API?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use TOTP (time-based one-time passwords). The server creates a secret for the user, shows it as a QR code, and from then on login needs the password plus a 6-digit code from the app, which the server checks with the same secret.

How it works:
Setup: generate a secret (otplib or speakeasy), show a QR code, store the secret encrypted
Confirm: user enters a code, the server verifies it before turning 2FA on
Login step 1: password OK, return a short "2FA pending" token, not the real one
Login step 2: verify the 6-digit code, then issue the real session or JWT
Backup codes: one-time codes, stored hashed, for a lost phone

Example: A teacher's password leaks in another site's breach. The attacker logs in with the right password but cannot get past the 6-digit code, so the account stays safe.

Common mistake: Issuing the full access token after the password step and checking the code only in the UI. An attacker just calls the API directly and skips the 2FA screen.

Interview tip: Mention allowing a small time window (one step before and after) for clock drift, and rate-limiting code attempts, since there are only a million possible codes.

questions.question: How does a client usually send a JWT to an Express API when not using cookies?
options: In the URL, like /api/me?token=...
In the request body of every GET request
In the Authorization header, as "Bearer <token>"
In the User-Agent header
questions.correctAnswer: In the Authorization header, as "Bearer <token>"
questions.answer:
Why C: The Authorization header with the Bearer scheme is the standard place for access tokens.

Why not A: URLs end up in browser history, server logs and analytics, so tokens there leak easily.

Why not B: GET requests should not rely on a body, and many clients drop it.

Why not D: User-Agent describes the browser or client, it is not for credentials.

questions.question: What does jwt.verify(token, secret) do when the token has expired?
options: Returns null
Throws a TokenExpiredError
Returns the payload with an expired: true flag
Refreshes the token automatically
questions.correctAnswer: Throws a TokenExpiredError
questions.answer:
Why B: jsonwebtoken checks the exp claim and throws TokenExpiredError if the time has passed.

Why not A: verify throws on any invalid token, it never returns null.

Why not C: There is no expired flag. An expired token is simply rejected.

Why not D: jsonwebtoken never creates new tokens during verify.

questions.question: Why should a password reset token be stored as a hash in the database?
options: Hashing makes the token shorter to email
MongoDB cannot store random strings
So the token expires automatically
If the database leaks, the stored values cannot be used to reset accounts
questions.correctAnswer: If the database leaks, the stored values cannot be used to reset accounts
questions.answer:
Why D: The email holds the real token and the database holds only its hash, so a leaked database does not give anyone usable reset links.

Why not A: The hash is not what you email, and length does not matter here.

Why not B: MongoDB stores strings of any kind.

Why not C: Expiry comes from a separate expires field, not from hashing.

questions.question: Any teacher can edit any course by changing the course id in the URL. What is this vulnerability called?
options: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
CSRF
XSS
SQL injection
questions.correctAnswer: IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference)
questions.answer:
Why A: The API uses an id from the request without checking that the logged-in user may access that object.

Why not B: CSRF tricks a user's browser into sending a request, it is not about missing ownership checks.

Why not C: XSS runs attacker scripts in other users' browsers.

Why not D: There is no injected query here, just a missing permission check.

Fix: Include owner: req.user._id in the query, or compare the owner before updating.

questions.question: What happens with jwt.sign({ id }, secret) when you pass no expiresIn option?
options: The token expires after 1 hour by default
The token expires when the server restarts
The token never expires
jwt.sign throws an error
questions.correctAnswer: The token never expires
questions.answer:
Why C: Without expiresIn (or an exp claim), the token has no expiry and stays valid until the secret changes.

Why not A: jsonwebtoken has no default expiry time.

Why not B: Tokens are stateless. A restart does not affect them unless the secret changes.

Why not D: An expiry is optional, so sign works without it.

Fix: Always set expiresIn, for example "15m" or "1d".

questions.question: A protect middleware uses jwt.decode(token) instead of jwt.verify(token, secret). What is the risk?
options: Tokens are verified twice, making requests slow
Nothing, decode and verify do the same thing
Expired tokens are rejected too early
Anyone can create a fake token with any user id, because the signature is never checked
questions.correctAnswer: Anyone can create a fake token with any user id, because the signature is never checked
questions.answer:
Why D: decode only reads the payload. Without checking the signature, an attacker can write their own token claiming to be an admin.

Why not A: decode does no verification at all, let alone twice.

Why not B: verify checks the signature and expiry, decode checks nothing.

Why not C: decode ignores expiry completely, so expired tokens are accepted, not rejected.

questions.question: What does the helmet middleware do, and which headers does it set?
questions.answer:
Short answer: helmet sets a group of HTTP security headers with one line, app.use(helmet()). They tell browsers to block common attacks like clickjacking, MIME sniffing and some kinds of script injection.

How it works: Main headers:
Content-Security-Policy: which sources scripts, styles and images may load from
Strict-Transport-Security: always use HTTPS for this site
X-Frame-Options: stops your pages being shown inside other sites' frames
X-Content-Type-Options nosniff: browsers must trust your Content-Type
Referrer-Policy: limits what URL info is sent to other sites
Removes X-Powered-By: hides that the server runs Express

Example: Run curl -I on your API before and after adding helmet. Before, you see "X-Powered-By: Express". After, you see a dozen protective headers and that one is gone.

Common mistake: Thinking helmet makes the API "secure". Headers help the browser, but they do nothing against bad auth, injection or missing validation on the server.

Interview tip: Mention that a strict Content-Security-Policy matters most for apps that serve HTML, and that for a JSON-only API helmet's defaults are usually fine as they are.
questions.codeSnippet:
const helmet = require('helmet');
app.use(helmet());

questions.question: How does express-rate-limit work, and how would you choose limits for login versus normal API routes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: It counts requests per key (the client IP by default) in a time window and returns 429 Too Many Requests when the count is over the limit. Use a strict limit on sensitive routes and a looser one for the rest.

How it works:
windowMs and limit: for example 300 requests per 15 minutes
Headers: tells clients how many requests are left
Store: memory by default, Redis when you run several instances
keyGenerator: can use the user id for logged-in routes instead of the IP
skipSuccessfulRequests: count only failed logins

Example: General API: 300 per 15 minutes per IP. Login: 10 per 15 minutes, counting only failures. Forgot password: 3 per hour per email. Normal users never notice, but scripts get blocked fast.

Common mistake: Using the in-memory store with 3 server instances. Each one counts separately, so the real limit is three times bigger than you think, and it resets on every deploy.

Interview tip: Mention that rate limits protect your costs too, like email sending and paid AI or SMS APIs, not just your login page.

questions.question: Why does an Express app on Render, Heroku or behind Nginx need app.set("trust proxy"), and what goes wrong without it or with it set to true?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Behind a proxy, every request reaches Express from the proxy's address over plain HTTP. trust proxy tells Express to read the real client IP and protocol from X-Forwarded-For and X-Forwarded-Proto.

How it works:
Not set: req.ip is the proxy's IP, req.secure is false, secure cookies may not be sent
Set to 1: trust exactly one proxy hop, read the client IP from the header it adds
Set to true: trust every hop, so a client can fake X-Forwarded-For
Rate limits: depend on req.ip, so this setting decides whether they work

Example: Without trust proxy, the rate limiter sees all users as one IP. After 300 requests in 15 minutes, the whole site returns 429 for everyone. express-rate-limit even logs a warning about this.

Common mistake: Setting trust proxy to true to silence that warning. Attackers can then send a new fake IP with every request and never hit the limit.

Interview tip: Say you set it to the number of proxies you really have, and check req.ip in logs after deploy. It is a small setting that shows production experience.
questions.codeSnippet: app.set('trust proxy', 1); // Render / Heroku: one proxy in front

questions.question: What is XSS, and how can it happen in a MERN app even though React escapes output?
questions.answer: Short answer: XSS (cross-site scripting) is when an attacker's script runs in another user's browser on your site. React escapes normal text, but XSS still happens when you insert raw HTML, build URLs from user data, or serve user content from your own domain. How it works: Ways it slips in: dangerouslySetInnerHTML: rendering user-written HTML or Markdown without sanitizing Links: href={user.website} with "javascript:..." as the value Uploaded HTML or SVG: served from your domain and opened directly Server-rendered pages: templates that print data without escaping Example: A comment system allows formatting and renders it with dangerouslySetInnerHTML. A user posts , and every reader's cookie is sent to the attacker. Common mistake: Trying to block XSS with your own regex that removes "
questions.codeSnippet:
import DOMPurify from 'dompurify';

<div dangerouslySetInnerHTML={{ __html: DOMPurify.sanitize(comment.html) }} />

questions.question: What is CSRF, and when does an Express API need protection against it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: CSRF (cross-site request forgery) tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending a request to your site from another site. It only works when the browser adds credentials automatically, which means cookie-based auth.

How it works:
Cookie auth: the browser attaches cookies automatically, so CSRF is a risk
Bearer tokens: the attacker's page cannot add your Authorization header, so CSRF does not apply
sameSite Lax or Strict: browsers do not send the cookie on most cross-site POSTs
Extra layers: CSRF tokens, checking the Origin header, never changing data with GET

Example: A user is logged in to your app. They open a forum post with a hidden form that auto-submits POST /api/account/delete to your API. If your cookie is sameSite 'none' and you have no other check, the account is deleted.

Common mistake: Using sameSite 'none' for a cross-domain setup and adding no other CSRF protection. That cookie is sent on cross-site requests again.

Interview tip: Say that with sameSite 'none', you add an Origin check or a CSRF token on state-changing routes, and you keep GET requests read-only.

questions.question: Someone accidentally pushed the .env file with the JWT secret and database password to GitHub. What do you do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Treat the secrets as stolen. Rotate every leaked secret first, then remove the file from the repo and stop it from coming back. Deleting the commit alone is not enough.

How it works: Steps in order:
Rotate: new database password, new JWT secret, new email and API keys
Redeploy: update the env vars on the host and restart
Side effect: a new JWT secret logs everyone out, which is fine
Clean: git rm --cached .env, add .env to .gitignore, commit
History: rewrite with git filter-repo if the repo is public, but assume it was already copied
Check: look at database and provider logs for unusual access

Example: Bots scan public GitHub repos for keys within minutes. A leaked cloud key can create servers for crypto mining and leave a huge bill by the next morning.

Common mistake: Making the repo private and moving on. Forks, clones and caches may already have the file, and the old secrets still work.

Interview tip: Mention prevention: a committed .env.example with fake values, secret scanning on GitHub, and a pre-commit hook. Remote teams see this as basic professionalism.
questions.codeSnippet:
# .env.example (safe to commit)
MONGO_URI=CHANGE_ME
JWT_SECRET=CHANGE_ME
CLIENT_URL=http://localhost:5173

questions.question: How can a single request slow down or crash an Express server, and how do body limits, timeouts and safe regex protect it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Since Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, one expensive request can block every user. Huge bodies, slow regex patterns and endless processing are the usual ways. Limits and timeouts keep each request's cost small.

How it works:
Body limits: express.json({ limit: '100kb' }) for normal routes
Upload limits: multer fileSize and files
ReDoS: a regex like /^(a+)+$/ on crafted input takes seconds or minutes
Server timeouts: server.requestTimeout and headersTimeout close slow clients
Pagination caps: never return unlimited results

Example: A validation regex for emails, copied from an old blog post, takes 10 seconds on a crafted 50 character string. An attacker sends it 20 times and the API stops answering anyone.

Common mistake: Raising the JSON limit to 50mb for the whole app because one import route needed it. Every endpoint now accepts huge bodies.

Interview tip: Mention using a bigger limit only on the specific route that needs it, and using well-tested validator libraries instead of your own complex regex.

questions.question: What are prototype pollution and HTTP parameter pollution, and how do they affect Express apps?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Prototype pollution is when user input with keys like __proto__ changes the base Object prototype, giving every object in the app new properties. Parameter pollution is sending the same query key many times so a value becomes an array your code does not expect.

How it works:
Prototype pollution: a deep merge of { "__proto__": { "isAdmin": true } } into an object
Result: every object now seems to have isAdmin true
Parameter pollution: ?role=user&role=admin gives an array
Result: string checks pass or crash in surprising ways
Defences: validate with a schema, never deep-merge raw input, and normalize query values

Example: A settings route deep-merges req.body into a config object using an old merge helper. An attacker sends the __proto__ payload, and a later if (user.isAdmin) check is true for everyone.

Common mistake: Thinking JSON.parse is the problem. It creates an own property called __proto__, and the damage happens when a merge function copies it into an object.

Interview tip: Mention using Object.create(null) or Map for dictionaries built from user keys, and keeping libraries like lodash up to date, since several merge bugs were fixed there.

questions.question: Why is CORS not a security feature for protecting your API from attackers?
questions.answer:
Short answer: CORS only tells browsers which websites may read your API's responses. Tools like curl, Postman, scripts and servers ignore CORS completely, so it cannot stop anyone from calling your API directly.

How it works:
Browser rule: a page on site A cannot read responses from API B unless B allows A
Not enforced on servers: any non-browser client can call any endpoint
Preflight: browsers send OPTIONS first for some requests
What protects you: authentication, authorization, validation and rate limits

Example: An API sets CORS origin to only https://askedin.vercel.app and thinks admin routes are now safe. Someone runs curl with a stolen token and gets the data anyway.

Common mistake: Setting origin: '*' together with credentials: true, or reflecting any Origin back with credentials. Then any website a user visits can make logged-in requests and read the replies.

Interview tip: Say CORS protects users (their browser data) more than your server. That one sentence clears up a confusion many developers have, and interviewers notice it.

questions.question: Before handing an Express API over to a client, what would you check in a quick security review?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Go through a short checklist covering secrets, auth, input, output, dependencies and deployment. Most real incidents come from a few common gaps, not from rare attacks.

How it works: A practical checklist:
Secrets: none in git, strong JWT secret, keys rotated, .env.example only
Auth: hashed passwords, token expiry, protect on every private route, ownership checks
Input: validation on every route, body limits, no raw req.body or req.query in queries
Output: no password hashes or stack traces in responses
Headers and abuse: helmet, CORS with an exact origin, rate limits on auth
Dependencies: npm audit, remove unused packages
Ops: HTTPS, trust proxy, backups, an admin password changed from the default

Real example: A freelance project passes all its feature tests, but the review finds the seeded admin still uses its demo password and test .http files in the repo contain a real password. Both are fixed before the client goes live.

Common mistake: Doing the review after launch, when changing secrets means logging out real users and fixing data.

Interview tip: Mention OWASP API Security Top 10 as your reference list. Clients and remote employers trust developers who use a known standard.

questions.question: Which package sets a group of HTTP security headers in an Express app with one line?
options: helmet
cors
morgan
bcrypt
questions.correctAnswer: helmet
questions.answer:
Why A: app.use(helmet()) adds headers like Strict-Transport-Security and X-Content-Type-Options.

Why not B: cors sets CORS headers only, to allow certain origins.

Why not C: morgan logs requests.

Why not D: bcrypt hashes passwords and has nothing to do with headers.

questions.question: An API on Render uses express-rate-limit (100 requests per 15 minutes) but does not set trust proxy. What happens on a busy day?
options: Each user gets their own limit, as intended
All users share one limit, because every request seems to come from the proxy's IP
The rate limiter is ignored behind a proxy
Only users with IPv6 addresses are limited
questions.correctAnswer: All users share one limit, because every request seems to come from the proxy's IP
questions.answer:
Why B: Without trust proxy, req.ip is the proxy's address for everyone, so all traffic counts against one key.

Why not A: The real client IPs are never read, so users are not separated.

Why not C: The limiter still runs, it just uses the wrong IP.

Why not D: The IP version does not matter, everyone appears as the proxy.

Fix: app.set("trust proxy", 1)

questions.question: Which cookie setting does the most to stop CSRF attacks on cookie-based auth?
options: httpOnly: true
maxAge: 15 minutes
sameSite: "lax" or "strict"
signed: true
questions.correctAnswer: sameSite: "lax" or "strict"
questions.answer:
Why C: With sameSite lax or strict, the browser does not attach the cookie to most cross-site requests, which is what CSRF depends on.

Why not A: httpOnly stops JavaScript from reading the cookie (helps against XSS), but the browser still sends it cross-site.

Why not B: A short lifetime reduces the time window, but the cookie is still sent while it is valid.

Why not D: Signing stops the cookie from being changed, not from being sent.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of stored XSS?
options: A user guesses another user's password
An attacker reads data with a stolen JWT
A request with ?role=admin&role=user crashes a route
A comment containing a script is saved and then runs in every reader's browser
questions.correctAnswer: A comment containing a script is saved and then runs in every reader's browser
questions.answer:
Why D: The malicious script is stored in your database and runs for every user who views it. That is stored XSS.

Why not A: Password guessing is a brute-force attack.

Why not B: Using a stolen token is session hijacking, not script injection.

Why not C: Repeating query keys is parameter pollution.

questions.question: A route deep-merges req.body into an existing object. An attacker sends { "__proto__": { "isAdmin": true } }. What can happen?
options: Nothing, JSON cannot contain __proto__
Only that one object gets isAdmin: true
Every plain object in the app can appear to have isAdmin: true
Express rejects the body with 400 automatically
questions.correctAnswer: Every plain object in the app can appear to have isAdmin: true
questions.answer:
Why C: An unsafe deep merge writes into Object.prototype, which every plain object inherits from. This is prototype pollution.

Why not A: JSON can contain a "__proto__" key, and JSON.parse keeps it as a normal property.

Why not B: The change goes to the shared prototype, not just one object.

Why not D: express.json() does not block this key, so validation is your job.

questions.question: Your API only allows CORS from https://myapp.com. Can an attacker's Node.js script on their own server still call your API?
options: Yes, CORS is only enforced by browsers
No, the server rejects requests from other origins
Only GET requests can get through
No, the preflight request blocks it
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, CORS is only enforced by browsers
questions.answer:
Why A: CORS is a browser rule about reading responses. Servers, curl and scripts do not apply it.

Why not B: The cors middleware only adds headers. It does not block requests by itself.

Why not C: Any method works from a script, not just GET.

Why not D: Only browsers send preflight requests, and a script can skip them.

Fix: Protect data with authentication, authorization and rate limits, not with CORS.

questions.question: What is a good folder structure for an Express API project?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Split the code by job: routes say which URL goes where, controllers handle the request and response, services hold business logic, models talk to the database, and middleware and utils hold shared helpers.

How it works: A common layout:
routes/: URL paths and middleware lists, no logic
controllers/: read req, call a service, send res
services/: business rules, reusable from routes, jobs and scripts
models/: Mongoose schemas
middleware/: auth, validation, error handler
config/ and utils/: env loading, database connection, helpers
app.js and server.js: app setup, and the listen call

Example: A bug in "quiz score calculation" is fixed in services/quizService.js. Every route and the nightly report that uses it get the fix, and nobody has to search through route files.

Common mistake: Putting everything in one 1,500-line app.js or in giant route files with queries inside. It works for a demo, but every change becomes risky.

Interview tip: For take-home assignments, a clear structure plus a README that explains it is often what gets you to the next round, even before the reviewer runs the code.
questions.codeSnippet:
server/
  app.js          server.js
  routes/         courseRoutes.js
  controllers/    courseController.js
  services/       courseService.js
  models/         Course.js
  middleware/     auth.js  validate.js  errorHandler.js
  config/         db.js

questions.question: Why separate controllers from services in an Express app, and what goes in each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Controllers deal with HTTP: reading the request, choosing the status code and sending JSON. Services deal with the business rules and the database. Keeping them apart makes the logic reusable and much easier to test.

How it works:
Controller: parse input, call service, map the result or error to HTTP
Service: knows nothing about req or res, takes plain values and returns plain values
Reuse: the same service is used by an API route, a cron job and a seed script
Testing: services can be unit-tested without starting Express

Example: submitQuiz(userId, answers) in quizService calculates the score and saves the attempt. The controller just calls it and returns 201. Later, a "bulk import of old attempts" script calls the same function.

Common mistake: Passing req and res into services. The service is then tied to Express, and you cannot reuse or test it on its own.

Interview tip: Say you do not add layers just for the sake of it. For a small CRUD route, a controller calling the model directly is fine; services pay off when there are real rules.

questions.question: How do you design one consistent JSON response format for both success and errors?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Pick one shape and use it everywhere. A popular one is { success, data, message } for success and { success: false, message, code, errors } for errors, with the HTTP status code still set correctly.

How it works:
success: true or false, easy to check
data: the payload, an object or a list
message: short text for toasts
code and errors: for programs and form fields on failure
meta: pagination info like page, limit and total
Helpers: small functions so nobody builds responses by hand

Example: The React app has one API helper. If success is false, it shows message in a toast and passes errors to the form. Every screen gets correct error handling for free.

Common mistake: Returning 200 with { success: false } for errors. Monitoring, caching and the browser all think the request worked. Keep real status codes as well as the success flag.

Interview tip: Mention that you write the format down in the README or API docs, so new team members and frontend developers follow it from day one.

questions.question: How do you add filtering, sorting and field selection to a list endpoint like GET /api/questions?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Read allowed query parameters, turn them into a safe MongoDB filter, a sort and a projection, and ignore or reject everything else. Keep the URL simple, like ?difficulty=hard&sort=-createdAt&fields=question,difficulty.

How it works:
Filters: copy only whitelisted keys into the filter object
Sort: a minus sign means descending, map it from a list of allowed values
Fields: allow a fixed set, never include password or internal fields
Pagination: page and limit with a cap
Search: a separate q parameter with escaped regex or a text index

Example: The question bank page filters by language and difficulty, sorts by newest, and asks only for the fields shown in the list. The response is a fraction of the full documents and loads fast on mobile.

Common mistake: Passing the whole req.query into find(). Users can then filter by any field, use operators, and force slow queries on unindexed fields.

Interview tip: Mention that each allowed filter and sort should have a matching index. Designing the API and the indexes together is a sign of senior thinking.

questions.question: How do you document an Express API so other developers can use it without asking you?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Write an OpenAPI (Swagger) spec and serve it with swagger-ui-express, or share a Postman collection. Add a README with setup steps, env variables, and the response and error format.

How it works:
OpenAPI spec: describes every endpoint, parameters, bodies and responses
swagger-ui-express: serves interactive docs at /api/docs
Postman or .http files: ready-to-run example requests
README: install, env vars, scripts, folder structure, test accounts
Keep in sync: generate docs from validation schemas where possible

Example: A frontend developer in another time zone opens /api/docs, tries POST /api/auth/login in the browser, sees the exact error shape, and builds the login page without waiting 8 hours for your reply.

Common mistake: Writing docs once and never updating them. Wrong docs are worse than none, because people trust them.

Interview tip: For remote jobs, say "I write docs for async teams". Good documentation is a top skill when people rarely share working hours.

questions.question: How do you design REST endpoints for actions that are not simple CRUD, like "publish a course" or "submit a quiz"?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a sub-resource or an action noun with POST, like POST /courses/:id/publish or POST /quizzes/:id/attempts. Choose names that read clearly and keep the action's rules in one place.

How it works: Common patterns:
State change: POST /courses/:id/publish, or PATCH /courses/:id with { status: 'published' }
Create a record of the action: POST /quizzes/:id/attempts
Commands: POST /auth/logout, POST /auth/forgot-password
Bulk: POST /questions/bulk-delete with a list of ids

Example: Publishing a course needs checks: at least 5 lessons, a price, an approved cover image. POST /courses/:id/publish keeps those rules in one endpoint, instead of letting any PATCH change the status field directly.

Common mistake: Using GET for actions, like GET /courses/5/publish. Link previews, crawlers and browser prefetching can trigger it by accident.

Interview tip: Say REST is a guideline, not a religion. Clear, predictable names matter more than pure resource nouns, and teams should stay consistent.

questions.question: An endpoint must send 1,000 emails or generate a large PDF. How do you design it so the request does not take minutes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Do not do slow work inside the request. Save a job, return 202 Accepted with a job id at once, and let a background worker do the work. The client checks the job status or gets notified when it is done.

How it works:
Request: validate, create the job, return 202 with { jobId }
Queue: BullMQ (Redis) or a jobs collection in MongoDB
Worker: a separate process that picks up jobs, with retries
Status: GET /jobs/:id returns pending, running, done or failed
Result: a download link or an email when finished

Example: An admin clicks "Send newsletter to 5,000 users". The API answers in 50 ms with 202. The worker sends emails in batches, respecting the provider's rate limit, and the dashboard shows "3,200 / 5,000 sent".

Common mistake: Doing it in the request with a long timeout. Proxies like Render or Nginx cut connections after a limit, the user clicks again, and the emails are sent twice.

Interview tip: Mention idempotency (the same job is not created twice) and that free hosts may sleep, so a sleeping worker needs a paid instance or an external job service.

questions.question: You get a take-home assignment: "Build a REST API in Express". What makes the submission stand out to a remote reviewer?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Make it easy to run, easy to read, and clearly correct. Reviewers spend 15 to 30 minutes per submission, so the README, structure, validation, error handling and a few tests matter as much as the features.

How it works: What reviewers look for:
README: one-command setup, env example, endpoint list, decisions and trade-offs
Structure: routes, controllers, services, models, middleware
Correctness: validation, proper status codes, consistent JSON errors
Security basics: hashed passwords, no secrets in git, protected routes
Tests: a few Jest + Supertest tests for the main flows
Extras: seed script, Postman collection or Swagger, Docker if asked

Real example: Two candidates build the same task. One has more features but no README and crashes on bad input. The other has fewer features, clean errors and 8 tests. The second one gets the interview.

Common mistake: Over-engineering with microservices and five design patterns. It reads as "can't judge scope", which is a red flag for remote teams.

Interview tip: Add a short "What I would do with more time" section. It shows judgement and gives the reviewer topics for the follow-up call.

questions.question: How do you receive webhooks (for example from Stripe) in an Express app correctly?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Give the webhook route the raw body so you can verify the provider's signature, answer 2xx quickly, handle each event only once, and do the heavy work in the background.

How it works:
Raw body: express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }) on that route only
Signature: verify with the provider's SDK and your webhook secret
Order: mount the webhook route before app.use(express.json())
Idempotency: store the event id, skip events you already processed
Speed: respond 200 within seconds, or the provider retries

Example: Stripe sends checkout.session.completed. The route verifies the signature, saves the event id, marks the order as paid and replies 200. If Stripe retries the same event, it is ignored.

Common mistake: Parsing the body with express.json() first. The signature check uses the exact raw bytes, so it always fails with "No signatures found matching the expected signature".

Interview tip: Mention never trusting webhook data without signature verification, since the URL is public and anyone could send fake "payment succeeded" events.

questions.question: When is plain REST not enough for a feature, and how do you choose between polling, SSE and WebSockets in an Express app?
questions.answer:
Short answer: REST is request and response, so the server cannot push updates by itself. For live data, choose by direction and frequency: polling for rare updates, SSE for server-to-client streams, WebSockets for two-way, frequent messages.

How it works:
Polling: client asks every N seconds, simplest, wastes requests
Long polling: server holds the request until there is news
SSE: one long HTTP response, server to client only, auto reconnect
WebSockets / Socket.IO: two-way, low latency, needs more setup and scaling care
Scaling: with many servers, use Redis pub/sub so every instance gets the events

Example: Order status updates every few minutes: polling every 30 seconds is fine. A live quiz leaderboard: SSE. A chat with typing indicators: Socket.IO.

Common mistake: Choosing WebSockets for everything. They need sticky sessions or an adapter when scaling, and some hosts or proxies need extra settings for them.

Interview tip: Say you start with the simplest option that meets the need and upgrade when it hurts. That pragmatic answer is exactly what startups and remote teams want.

questions.question: In a routes, controllers and services structure, where should the main business rules live?
options: In the routes files
In services
In the error handler
In app.js
questions.correctAnswer: In services
questions.answer:
Why B: Services hold the business logic, so it can be reused and tested without HTTP.

Why not A: Routes should only map URLs to middleware and controllers.

Why not C: The error handler formats errors, it should not contain business rules.

Why not D: app.js wires the app together, it should stay small.

questions.question: An endpoint starts sending emails to 5,000 users, which takes several minutes. What is the best response?
options: Wait until all emails are sent, then return 200
Return 500 so the client tries again later
Return 202 Accepted with a job id, and send the emails in the background
Return 204 and never tell the client what happened
questions.correctAnswer: Return 202 Accepted with a job id, and send the emails in the background
questions.answer:
Why C: 202 means "accepted for processing". The client gets a quick answer and can check the job status.

Why not A: Proxies and browsers time out long requests, and users click again, causing duplicates.

Why not B: 500 means the server failed, which is not true.

Why not D: The client has no way to know if the work finished or failed.

questions.question: In GET /api/questions?sort=-createdAt, what does the minus sign usually mean?
options: Exclude the createdAt field from the response
Remove items without createdAt
Sort by createdAt only for deleted items
Sort by createdAt in descending order, newest first
questions.correctAnswer: Sort by createdAt in descending order, newest first
questions.answer:
Why D: A leading minus is the common convention for descending order, and Mongoose's sort() understands it directly.

Why not A: Excluding a field is a projection, usually a separate fields parameter.

Why not B: Sorting never removes documents.

Why not C: The sign is about direction, not deleted items.

questions.question: What is an OpenAPI (Swagger) specification used for?
options: Describing an API's endpoints, inputs and responses in a standard format
Encrypting API traffic
Load testing an API
Replacing Express routes
questions.correctAnswer: Describing an API's endpoints, inputs and responses in a standard format
questions.answer:
Why A: OpenAPI is a standard file format for API documentation, and tools turn it into interactive docs and client code.

Why not B: Encryption comes from HTTPS (TLS).

Why not C: Load testing uses tools like autocannon or k6.

Why not D: The spec describes routes, you still write them in Express.

questions.question: Stripe webhook signature checks always fail with "No signatures found matching the expected signature". The app uses app.use(express.json()) at the top. What is the likely cause?
options: The webhook secret must be Base64 encoded first
The body was already parsed into an object, so the raw bytes needed for the signature are lost
Stripe only sends webhooks over plain HTTP
Express strips the Stripe-Signature header
questions.correctAnswer: The body was already parsed into an object, so the raw bytes needed for the signature are lost
questions.answer:
Why B: The signature is computed over the exact raw body. Once express.json() parses it, re-serializing gives different bytes and the check fails.

Why not A: The SDK uses the secret exactly as Stripe shows it.

Why not C: Stripe sends webhooks over HTTPS.

Why not D: Express does not remove headers.

Fix: Use express.raw({ type: "application/json" }) on the webhook route, registered before express.json().

questions.question: A list endpoint passes ?fields= straight into .select(req.query.fields). What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, Mongoose ignores unknown fields
The query always returns all fields
Field selection only works with lean()
A user can request ?fields=password and get password hashes in the response
questions.correctAnswer: A user can request ?fields=password and get password hashes in the response
questions.answer:
Why D: Without a whitelist, users can select any field, including sensitive ones. Even select: false fields can be forced in with "+password".

Why not A: Real field names like password are not unknown, so they are returned.

Why not B: select() does limit the fields, it just limits them to what the attacker asks.

Why not C: select() works with or without lean().

Fix: Keep a list of allowed fields and filter the requested ones against it.

questions.question: You have only a little time to write tests for an Express API. What do you test first?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Test the flows that would hurt most if they broke: login and signup, permission checks on protected routes, and the main money or data flow. For each, test one success case and the most likely failure cases.

How it works: A short priority list:
Auth: signup, login with right and wrong password, a protected route without a token
Permissions: a normal user calling an admin route gets 403
Validation: a bad body gets 400 with errors
Core feature: the main create and read flow works end to end
Bugs: every fixed bug gets a test so it never comes back

Example: Ten Supertest tests covering auth, permissions and quiz submission run in 5 seconds and catch most mistakes before a deploy. That is far more useful than 100% coverage of helper functions.

Common mistake: Testing only the happy path. Most production bugs come from missing tokens, wrong ids and bad input, which happy-path tests never touch.

Interview tip: Say "I test behaviour through the API, not implementation details". It shows you write tests that survive refactoring.

questions.question: How do you test a protected Express route with Jest and Supertest?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create a test user and get a token in beforeAll (by calling the login route or signing a JWT directly), then send it in the Authorization header with .set(). Also test the same route without a token and with the wrong role.

How it works:
Setup: create users in a test database in beforeAll
Token: request(app).post('/api/auth/login') or jwt.sign with the test secret
Call: request(app).get('/api/me').set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`)
Assert: status, body shape, and that no password field is returned
Negative cases: no token gives 401, wrong role gives 403

Example: Three tests for GET /api/admin/stats: admin gets 200, a normal user gets 403, no token gets 401. Together they prove the route is protected correctly.

Common mistake: Testing against your real development or production database. Tests create and delete data and can wipe things you need.

Interview tip: Mention exporting app from app.js without calling listen(), so Supertest can run it in memory without opening a port.

questions.question: How do you keep test data separate from development data and make each test start clean?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a separate test database (in-memory or a dedicated one), connect to it only when NODE_ENV is test, and clear the collections before or after each test so tests do not depend on each other.

How it works:
Separate DB: mongodb-memory-server, or a MONGO_URI_TEST pointing to a test database
Guard: refuse to run tests if the URI does not contain "test"
Clean: deleteMany({}) on each collection in beforeEach or afterEach
Factories: small helper functions to create a user or a course with defaults
Close: disconnect in afterAll, so Jest exits cleanly

Example: Test A creates a user with ali@example.com. Without cleanup, test B tries to sign up the same email and fails with 409, but only when both run, which makes a "flaky" test.

Common mistake: Tests that rely on the order they run in. They pass on your laptop and fail in CI, where Jest may run files in parallel or in a different order.

Interview tip: Mention the safety guard. A test suite that deletes data must never be able to point at a real database, and saying so shows you have thought about accidents.

questions.question: Walk through deploying an Express API to Render (or a similar platform) step by step.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Push the code to GitHub, create a Web Service from the repo, set the root folder, build and start commands, add the environment variables, and check the logs and a health endpoint after the first deploy.

How it works: The steps:
Code ready: listens on process.env.PORT, start script is node server.js
Service: new Web Service, connect the GitHub repo, set the root directory (for example server)
Commands: build npm install, start npm start
Env vars: MONGO_URI, JWT_SECRET, CLIENT_URL, NODE_ENV=production
Database: allow the host's IPs in Atlas Network Access
Verify: open /api/health and test a login from the deployed frontend
Auto deploy: every push to main deploys again

Example: The first deploy fails with "MongoServerSelectionError". Atlas network access did not allow the server. Adding the right IP access fixes it, and the next deploy goes live.

Common mistake: Forgetting to update CLIENT_URL after deploying the frontend, so CORS blocks every request from the live site.

Interview tip: Mention that pushing to main deploys immediately, so you use a branch and pull requests for risky changes, or a staging service.

questions.question: What is a health check endpoint, and what should it check?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A health check is a small endpoint, like GET /api/health, that the hosting platform or a monitor calls to see if the app is alive and ready. It should be fast, need no login, and say whether the app can serve requests.

How it works:
Liveness: is the process running and answering (always 200 if it can respond)
Readiness: can it do real work, for example is the database connected
Speed: no heavy queries, answer within milliseconds
Response: status plus useful info like uptime or version, never secrets
Use: deploy checks, uptime monitors, load balancers

Example: After a deploy, Render calls /api/health. If the database is down it returns 503, the platform keeps the old version running, and users never see the broken one.

Common mistake: A health check that runs a heavy aggregation. Monitors call it every few seconds, so it adds constant load and can slow the real API.

Interview tip: Mention a free uptime monitor (like UptimeRobot) that alerts you by email when health fails, so you find out before your users or client do.

questions.question: On a free hosting tier, the first request after some idle time takes 30 to 50 seconds. Why, and what can you do about it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Free web services are put to sleep after a period with no traffic (around 15 minutes on Render's free tier). The next request has to wait for the service to start again, which is called a cold start.

How it works: Options:
Upgrade: a paid instance stays always on, the real fix for production
Show it in the UI: a friendly "Waking up the server..." message instead of a frozen page
Faster start: fewer heavy imports at startup, connect to the database quickly
Keep-alive pings: possible, but they may break the host's free-tier rules and only hide the problem

Example: A client opens the live demo in the morning and the login button seems broken for 40 seconds. Adding a loading message and explaining the free-tier limit in the handover notes avoids a worried email.

Common mistake: Thinking the code got slow and spending hours optimizing routes. The delay is the platform starting the server, not your code.

Interview tip: Say you explain hosting trade-offs to clients in plain words: free tiers are for demos, while a paying business needs an always-on instance.

questions.question: How do you set up GitHub Actions to run your Express API tests on every push or pull request?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Add a workflow file in .github/workflows that checks out the code, installs Node, runs npm ci and npm test on each push and pull request. Store any test secrets in GitHub Secrets, never in the YAML file.

How it works:
Trigger: on push and pull_request to main
Steps: checkout, setup-node with a fixed version and npm cache, npm ci, npm test
Database: mongodb-memory-server, or a MongoDB service container
Secrets: ${{ secrets.JWT_SECRET_TEST }} from the repo settings
Protection: require the check to pass before merging to main

Example: A teammate opens a pull request that breaks login. The red X in the pull request shows the failed test, so the bug never reaches main, which would have deployed it to production at once.

Common mistake: Using npm install instead of npm ci. npm ci installs the exact versions from package-lock.json, so CI tests what you actually ship.

Interview tip: For remote roles, mention CI as part of your normal workflow. It shows you can work safely in a team where nobody watches your screen.
questions.codeSnippet:
# .github/workflows/test.yml
name: test
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    defaults: { run: { working-directory: server } }
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 24, cache: npm, cache-dependency-path: server/package-lock.json }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm test
        env:
          JWT_SECRET: ${{ secrets.JWT_SECRET_TEST }}

questions.question: How do you load test an Express API, and how do you read the results?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use a tool like autocannon or k6 to send many requests at once against a staging copy, then read requests per second, latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99) and error counts. Find the first thing that breaks and fix that.

How it works:
Run: npx autocannon -c 50 -d 20 https://staging.example.com/api/courses
Throughput: requests per second the API can handle
Latency: p50 is the typical request, p99 is the slowest 1%
Errors: timeouts and non-2xx responses under load
Watch: CPU, memory and database metrics while the test runs

Example: GET /api/courses handles 400 requests per second with p99 of 80 ms. The quiz submit route drops to 30 per second with p99 of 2 seconds. explain() shows a missing index, and after adding it the route handles 250 per second.

Common mistake: Load testing production or a free-tier database. You can take the live site down or hit the provider's limits.

Interview tip: Mention that averages hide problems. Say "p95 and p99 matter most, because those are the users who complain".
questions.codeSnippet: npx autocannon -c 50 -d 20 -H "Authorization=Bearer TEST_TOKEN" https://staging.example.com/api/courses

questions.question: Everything works locally, but after deploying, the browser shows CORS errors on every API call. How do you debug it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Look at the actual failing request first. A "CORS error" often hides a different problem: the server crashed, returned a 502 or 404, or CLIENT_URL does not exactly match the frontend's origin.

How it works: Check in this order:
Network tab: the real status code, 502 or 503 means the server is down or sleeping
Server logs: crashes at startup, missing env vars
Exact origin: https://askedin.vercel.app with no trailing slash and the right protocol
Env var: CLIENT_URL set on the host and the service restarted after changing it
Credentials: credentials: true on the server if the frontend sends cookies
Preflight: OPTIONS requests must also get the CORS headers

Real example: The API on Render crashed because of a missing JWT_SECRET. The platform's error page has no CORS headers, so the browser reported "CORS policy" even though the real error was a crash.

Common mistake: Changing cors() to allow every origin to "fix" it. It hides the real cause and opens the API to every website.

Interview tip: Say you read the server logs before touching CORS settings. It is a short sentence that shows a calm debugging process.

questions.question: A deploy just broke production. How do you roll back quickly, and how do you make future releases safer?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Roll back first, investigate second. Redeploy the last working version from the host's dashboard or by reverting the commit, check that the site works, then find the cause calmly.

How it works:
Rollback: Render, Railway and Vercel can redeploy a previous build in one click
git revert: creates a new commit that undoes the bad one, safe for shared branches
Database changes: make them backward compatible, add fields first and remove old ones later
Feature flags: ship code turned off, then turn it on without a deploy
Staging: test on a copy before production
Smaller releases: easier to find what broke

Example: A release changes how quiz scores are saved and the dashboard crashes. The developer redeploys the previous build in 2 minutes, then finds the bug locally with the same data and ships a fix an hour later.

Common mistake: Trying to fix forward under pressure with quick patches straight to main. Each rushed patch can add new bugs while users wait.

Interview tip: Mention that you note what happened afterwards (a short postmortem) without blaming anyone. Remote teams value this culture a lot.
questions.codeSnippet:
git revert <bad-commit-sha>
git push origin main   # auto-deploys the fixed state

questions.question: Which library lets Jest tests send HTTP requests to an Express app without starting a real server on a port?
options: nodemon
axios
supertest
morgan
questions.correctAnswer: supertest
questions.answer:
Why C: supertest takes the app object and calls it in memory, then lets you check status, headers and body.

Why not A: nodemon restarts the server during development, it does not test.

Why not B: axios needs a running server with a real URL.

Why not D: morgan logs requests.

questions.question: On a free hosting plan, why does the first request in the morning take about 40 seconds?
options: The database rebuilds its indexes every night
The service was put to sleep after being idle and must start again
Express clears its route cache at midnight
The free plan only allows one request per minute
questions.correctAnswer: The service was put to sleep after being idle and must start again
questions.answer:
Why B: Free services sleep after a period without traffic, so the first request waits for a cold start.

Why not A: MongoDB does not rebuild indexes every night.

Why not C: Express has no route cache that expires.

Why not D: Free plans limit hours and resources, not one request per minute.

questions.question: What should a health check endpoint like GET /api/health do?
options: Run a full report so you know everything works
Require an admin token to stay private
Return all environment variables for debugging
Answer quickly with a status, optionally checking that the database is connected
questions.correctAnswer: Answer quickly with a status, optionally checking that the database is connected
questions.answer:
Why D: Monitors call it often, so it must be fast and simple, and a quick database check shows readiness.

Why not A: Heavy work on every check adds constant load.

Why not B: Platforms and monitors call it without login, so it must be public and contain nothing sensitive.

Why not C: Environment variables include secrets and must never be exposed.

questions.question: In a GitHub Actions workflow, where should a secret like a test JWT secret be stored?
options: In GitHub repository secrets, used as ${{ secrets.NAME }}
Written directly in the workflow YAML file
In a committed .env file
In the README
questions.correctAnswer: In GitHub repository secrets, used as ${{ secrets.NAME }}
questions.answer:
Why A: Repository secrets are encrypted, hidden in logs, and injected only when the workflow runs.

Why not B: The workflow file is in the repo, so anyone with access can read it.

Why not C: Committed .env files leak secrets to everyone with repo access, forever in history.

Why not D: The README is public documentation.

questions.question: A load test shows average latency 20 ms but p99 latency 2,000 ms. What does that tell you?
options: The API is fast for everyone, the p99 number can be ignored
The load test tool is broken
Most requests are fast, but 1% are very slow and need investigation
The server is out of memory
questions.correctAnswer: Most requests are fast, but 1% are very slow and need investigation
questions.answer:
Why C: p99 is the time under which 99% of requests finish, so the slowest 1% take about 2 seconds. Averages hide this tail.

Why not A: At scale, 1% means many real users, often the most active ones.

Why not B: A big gap between average and p99 is common, not a tool error.

Why not D: It could be memory, but also a missing index, a slow external call or garbage collection. You need more data first.

questions.question: Right after a deploy, the browser reports a CORS error, and the Network tab shows status 502 for the API call. What is the most likely real problem?
options: The CORS origin list is missing the frontend URL
The API server is down or crashed, and the proxy's error page has no CORS headers
The browser cache is full
The request used the wrong HTTP method
questions.correctAnswer: The API server is down or crashed, and the proxy's error page has no CORS headers
questions.answer:
Why B: 502 comes from the platform's proxy when your app does not answer. That error page has no CORS headers, so the browser shows a CORS error.

Why not A: A wrong origin gives a normal response without the allow header, not a 502.

Why not C: Cache size does not cause 502 errors.

Why not D: A wrong method gives 404 or 405 from your app, not 502.

Fix: Check the server logs for a startup crash, such as a missing environment variable.
